title: Sydney shark attack hero wins world paddleboarding championship
text:
A volunteer lifeguard who helped save a woman attacked by a shark on a Sydney beach has won the world paddleboarding championship amid hurricane conditions.

Charlie Verco competed in the 27th Moloka'i 2 O'ahu Paddleboard World Championships in Hawaii on Sunday.

Almost 100 participants from around the world paddleboarded a 52-kilometre stretch of open ocean from Moloka'i to O'ahu in the central Pacific.

It included crossing the Kaiwi Channel, known as the 'Channel of Bones', which is home to sharks, jellyfish and other marine life.

The organisers described it as being "widely regarded as the sport's ultimate open-ocean endurance challenge", testing paddlers' skills, endurance and ocean knowledge.

The 24-year-old from Sydney won the event for the fourth time, finishing in 4 hours, 18 minutes and 3 seconds, breaking the world record.

The elite paddleboarder walked out of the water on foot smiling after finishing the race. (Supplied: Moloka'i 2 O'ahu Paddleboard World Championships)

"I'm so stoked, it's so incredible. I've never felt so good in body and mind after the race and it's extra special that I was able to set a record at the same time," he said in a post-race interview.

"I've put years and years of work into it training two to three time a day, six days a week."

Mr Verco, who regularly trains in the northern beaches and Sydney's east, was training when he helped save shark attack survivor Leah Stewart at Coogee Beach in June.

"It has definitely helped remind me that the ocean is something you have to respect," he said.

Shark attack victim update The 34-year-old's brother said she was awake, speaking with loved ones and her medical team and "remembers the whole event in detail".

" I'm hoping Leah is doing alright and I feel incredibly grateful that I get to have an experience like this in the ocean. "

Hurricane conditions

Mr Verco had to navigate through "really big swells" and "strong winds" caused by Category 1 Hurricane Fausto, which was heading towards the Hawaiian Islands.

Throughout the week, organisers had been monitoring the hurricane forecasts from the Central Pacific Hurricane Center in coordination with the United States Coast Guard and local emergency management partners.

"I think with the cyclone we were a little worried about impacting, but it managed to stay far enough away that there was just good wind behind us," Mr Verco said.

Supporting him along the way in the escort boat was his brother, and father, Jamie Verco, who said the beginning of the race was "quiet".

Mr Verco was supported by his father and brother in the escort boat. (Supplied: Moloka'i 2 O'ahu Paddleboard World Championships)

"The swell wasn't lining up with the wind at all and you have to be very patient not to burn a lot of energy trying to chase the swell that would take you in the wrong direction," he said.

"Through the middle of the channel he started to speed up and by the end he was really flying.

" About an hour and a half out he said he'd have a crack at the record and his brother just said, 'Yeah, go for it'. "

The paddleboarder's mother and sister were watching from home.

Jamie Verco said he was "so proud" of his son.

"He's worked so hard and he's a humble kid who's put in the hard yards and does all the work and he's got the rewards today," he said.

"He's been quietly pleased with himself I think."

Race organisers said more than 35 Australians competed in the prone paddleboard competition with Mr Verco, with 38-year-old Stewart Mclachlan coming in second and 28-year-old Stone Harrison in third.

Mr Verco said this year's focus was to not "get ahead of himself".

"My goal was just to have fun with it. It was the same attitude I had throughout all my training, is not to be so stressed out."

title: Veterinary students denied paid training
text:
For Gemima Rahman, completing her studies as a vet meant relocating more than 1,500km from Port Hedland to Perth.

Now in her postgraduate studies, the 24-year-old is specialising in large animals.

Ms Rahman said the financial strain of moving away from home meant missing out on experiences she would have loved to pursue.

Gemima Rahman is a postgraduate student at Murdoch University’s School of Veterinary Medicine in Western Australia. (Supplied: Murdoch University)

"I would have loved to have gone to the Northern Territory, over east to Victoria where there are large animal practices, but in saying that the cost to do so was not possible," Ms Rahman said.

The post-graduate student said a paid prac program would have reduced emotional and financial stress.

"Within our degree, they recommend working 10 hours around your study and practical hours," Ms Rahman said.

"Sometimes I would be at uni 8-4pm then I would work night shift until 1am, so it wouldn't leave much time for sleep and self-preservation."

She said this was another reason burnout was so common in her profession.

Veterinary students have been left out of the Commonwealth Prac Payment. (Supplied: Murdoch University)

"I think if the government were to help students like me, we would see not only a rise in more larger-animals veterinarians, but I also think burnout, which happens in students and graduates, would be reduced because they would have more financial backing," she said.

Veterinary studies not included in expansion

Ms Rahman's comments come after the prime minister recently announced the expansion of the Commonwealth Prac Payment scheme.

The scheme now has an additional 10 university courses, but not veterinary studies.

Students of clinical psychology, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech pathology, paramedicine, radiography, pharmacy, rehabilitation therapies, audiology and podiatry are now eligible for a $338.60 per week payment.

"Paid prac is already making a real difference — it's helping students with cost of living while they train and that's why we're expanding it," Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said.

One of Australia's best-known veterinary schools has since called on the federal government to extend the scheme to include veterinary students.

'Extremely disappointed'

Murdoch University vet school professor and dean of engagement Cristy Secombe said the WA-based school was disappointed veterinary students had been left out of the program, despite facing some of the longest placements.

"We're extremely disappointed we've been left out of the scheme, especially because vets provide an essential service," she said.

Murdoch University says veterinary students should have the same support as other healthcare professions. (Supplied: Murdoch University)

"Students complete 52 weeks of compulsory placements while training for a profession that was recognised by government as an essential service during the COVID-19 pandemic.

" We've got data where students have said it can cost them up to $1,000 a week for them to go out on placement regionally. "

Ms Secombe said she believed the financial pressure of placements was contributing to a shortage in the veterinary workforce regionally.

"The veterinary profession is in its ninth year of shortage, so we are clearly a profession in need," she said.

Murdoch University welcomes the expansion of the payment, but wants vet students to be included. (Supplied: Murdoch University)

" We want more vets out regionally, and want them to experience prac in the rural sectors but it is really hard for them because of financial pressures, so they just don't go. "

Australian Veterinary Association president Diana Barker said the recent emergence of H5N1 avian influenza and the crucial frontline role veterinarians played showed how essential the profession was to Australia's biosecurity.

Vet chanced upon first H5 bird flu case A walk along the beach with a friend turned into the significant discovery.

"Only five weeks ago vets were called to be at the front line of the nation's biosecurity to protect our agricultural industry, and then yet again we are not supported by the government," she said.

"We were in Canberra talking to ministers only a few weeks ago, and had feedback about our possible inclusion, so we fail to understand what it is veterinarians are not doing right."

Education Minister Jason Clare said expanding the prac payment scheme to allied health was the next logical step.

"These are areas where there are big skills shortages and where we expect there will be more shortages in the future," he said.

He did not say whether veterinary students would be included in the scheme in the future.

title: Quick hits: Wiggles star's daughter shines, netball 'cleaner' goes viral
text:
Two Aussie besties share a podium, a hometown hero fights his way to the final, and a very famous face wiggles his way into the stands.

Here are the quick hits from day three of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Cleaning up never looked so good

Every major sporting event has its surprise star.

Sometimes it's an underdog athlete. Sometimes it's a mascot. And sometimes it's a cleaner with a mop and a sense of rhythm.

A short clip from the Commonwealth Games netball venue has captured exactly why sport is about more than the result.

Loading Instagram content

A cleaner who danced as he mopped the court has become an unexpected crowd-pleaser on social media.

The routine, which was done to I Want To Break Free by Queen, had it all: the splits, the worm and twerking. If there were judges, he would have scored 10 out of 10.

Was the "cleaner" just a dancer with a mop employed to entertain the crowd?

That's for you to judge. Either way, he brought a lot of joy to people in the stadium.

2. Brilliant besties prove the power of friendship is real

With a medal each to their names, attention turned to Aussies Gemma Sellick and Victoria Belando Nicholson as they stepped up to be interviewed after the women's 100m backstroke S9 event.

But the pair had eyes only for each other, their friendship taking centre stage as they gushed about sharing a podium.

"This is my best friend," Sellick said, grinning ear to ear, a question from the media suddenly feeling rather inconsequential.

"This was not even a thought I had; I was not expecting this at all," Belando Nicholson told the ABC.

"To do it with my best friend is actually insane."

As they headed to pick up their medals, the pair were already planning a "debrief later tonight" to celebrate their silver and bronze medals.

3. Silver is sweet for Canada's Dolci after epic gymnastics comeback

The Arena in Glasgow was the venue for one of the maddest competitions at the Games so far: the men's all-around final at the artistic gymnastics.

At the end of the day, Flower of Scotland was on full blast (followed by the latest rendition of The Proclaimers' 500 Miles) as Reuben Ward became the first Scots gymnast to win the competition in Commonwealth Games history.

Jesse Moore also flew the flag, so to speak, as he became the latest Australian gymnastic medal-winner at these Games with a bronze, coming after he had to withdraw halfway through the Games four years ago with a shoulder injury.

But with respect, both these performances were left in the dramatic shadows by the competition of Canada's Felix Dolci.

Felix Dolci was down in 17th place in the men's all-around gymnastics final after falling off the pommel horse twice, before the Canadian made a miraculous recovery. (Getty I,mages: Francois Nel)

The men's all-around features all six disciplines: vault, rings, pommel horse, parallel bars, horizontal bars and floor exercise. Gymnasts are split into groups doing the six in different orders, maximising the drama.

Dolci was in a decent spot when he went on the pommel horse, but everything went pear-shaped as he fell off, twice. He ended up 17th out of 18 competitors after two rounds.

Game over, right? Wrong. A score of 14.200 on the vault, followed by 13.950 on the parallel bars, left him in with a vague hope.

And then he delivered on the horizontal bars, absolutely nailing his landing and scoring a whopping 14.500 to finish with the silver medal. Amazing stuff.

4. Hometown hero Goodburn not done yet

The men's 50m breaststroke is a fairly stacked event, with English legend Adam Ramsay-Peaty, Australia's Sam Williamson and South African speedster Michael Houlie all in the field.

But if you look beyond the very top times, you find Scottish swimmer Archie Goodburn.

The Edinburgh-born Goodburn was the British champion in 50 breaststroke in 2023, and had a chance of going to the Paris Olympics. But then he was diagnosed with three inoperable brain cancers in early 2024.

He was in the eighth and final heat on day three, up against Williamson.

Archie Goodburn of Scotland during the men's 50m breaststroke semifinals in Glasgow yesterday. (Getty: Rob Casey)

The 50m breaststroke is not quite the same "splash-and-dash" as the 50 freestyle, but it's not slow.

Williamson surged through to win in 26.75, with South Africa's Chris Smith second, and Goodburn made the home fans happy coming through for third.

He backed it up in the semifinal to squeeze into the final tomorrow morning (AEST) in lane one.

Regardless of his eventual placing, you could argue that no-one is flying the Saltire higher at these Games than Goodburn.

5. The Red Wiggle watches daughter star in wheelchair basketball

The Red Wiggle was wearing green and gold in support of daughter Georgia Munro-Cook. (ABC)

The Australian women's wheelchair basketball team notched its first win of the Games on day three, downing South Africa 20-5.

Georgia Munro-Cook was the star for the green and gold, finishing with 10 points in a dominant performance.

Watching on in Glasgow was her father, Murray, who, despite not sporting his famous red skivvy, will be a familiar face to many Australians.

The Red Wiggle was as proud as punch after his daughter's performance.

"She's worked so hard, the whole team has worked so hard, to see them get a win like that is just really exciting," he told ABC Sport.

Munro-Cook was over the Moon to have her mum and dad in the crowd, and said it was an interesting role reversal for the family.

"I think it's so funny, I used to go around watching him on stage, and now he's here watching me," she said.

title: 'Weekend DIY' flat-pack homes misleading consumers
text:
Steve Harris purchased a prefabricated tiny home for $26,000 in April, believing it was the cheap way to build a small hair salon for his wife's home business in Bunbury, 150km south of Perth.

It was promised to him as a "build-in-a-weekend" job, but it is still sitting deconstructed in his driveway.

"Our engineer rang us yesterday and said the glass on the doors is only four millimetres when it has to be five [millimetres thick]," he said.

"It has been pretty tough going."

The flat-packed home could end up costing him double what he paid, as the Bunbury local battles to get the structure approved under council and Australian building standards.

"I would suggest to anyone doing these prefab builds that they get all their ducks in a row."

An outdoor DIY garden shed for sale online. (Supplied)

The company Mr Harris purchased from appears to be Australian but uses kits made in Europe.

The company, which the ABC has chosen not to name, said DIY assembly varied according to the customer's experience, site conditions and preparation.

"We therefore would not suggest that every customer's installation experience will be identical," a spokesperson said.

Potential consumer law breach

Australia's tiny home industry has seen a 120 per cent increase in sales since 2021, as the housing crisis forces people to look to alternative housing solutions.

Consumer Protection is warning that companies marketing prefabricated flat-pack homes as being "assembled in a weekend" could be in breach of consumer law.

WA's Commissioner for Consumer Protection Trish Blake has cautioned people to be wary of "DIY" or "permit-free homes" claims.

Trish Blake says promises of "permit-free" flat-packed homes should be scrutinised. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

"People are looking at quick and easy ways to get accommodation options constructed, and we know that constructing a full home can take a minimum of a year, so these prefab pods and buildings are a great option, " Ms Blake said.

" But I cannot conceive of a prefabricated pod which would be entirely permit-free. "

A major issue with the DIY kits is that they are often made from overseas parts that do not meet Australian building standards.

Owners also need to get proper council building approvals, which can sometimes take months.

"If they are advertising them as permit-free, we will be looking at that very closely and looking at whether they are breaching consumer law for engaging in misleading and deceptive conduct," Ms Blake said.

"Electrical work and all the plumbing work can only be done by licensed electricians and plumbers; these are not the DIY elements of these buildings."

Mr Harris's tiny home was purchased in April but is yet to be unpacked. (ABC South West: Madigan Landry)

Standards not up to scratch

Bunbury builder Deon Attard said he was seeing increasing issues with tiny homes purchased overseas.

"We just did a commercial project where they brought 12 from China, and the quality just was not up to scratch," he said.

"By the time it's all said and done, they didn't actually save much money at all, and the quality of the finish was not actually delivered."

Bunbury-based builder Deon Attard advises working with professionals. (supplied)

He said "reworks" often needed to be done on houses built overseas, including drilling new holes and places to put electrical outlets and plugs.

"Australian building standards exist for a reason," he said.

Mr Attard is not against tiny homes but says interested buyers should look closer to home.

"Find a local modular or tiny home builder and work with them on the design of the product that suits your budget," he said.

title: Mayo wins All-Ireland title, ending 75-year 'curse'
text:
In one of the greatest upsets in Gaelic football history, Mayo has beaten Kerry in the All-Ireland football final in Dublin to break a 75-year title drought and end what some people call "the Mayo curse".

Whether the curse was hokum, a story or a real psychological issue that had simply bedevilled generations of Mayo footballers, the victory by 1-20 (23 points) to 1-17 (20 points) at Croke Park immediately drew a line under three quarters of a century of heartbreak and became one of the biggest headlines in Gaelic games history.

And one of the stars of the unlikely victory is a footballer who many think could be a generational talent although he has only just finished school, and is headed to the AFL.

The story goes that after beating Meath at Croke Park in the 1951 All-Ireland final, a jubilant Mayo team travelled home to the western province of Connacht on the back of a truck, celebrating the whole way.

While passing through the village of Foxford though, the players passed by a funeral that was taking place.

The local priest apparently took a dim view of the players continuing to celebrate while the funeral was taking place, placing a "curse" on the county, that it would not win the title again until all the team that played that day had died.

Mayo's 70-year wait goes on amid All-Ireland 'curse' Sporting curse or psychological barrier? Whatever it is, Mayo's All-Ireland Gaelic football title drought reaches 70 years after another final of blown chances against Tyrone at Croke Park.

After 1951, it took the Mayo senior team 38 years to return to the All-Ireland final. In total, before this year, it had played in 11 All-Ireland finals since 1951 and lost them all.

In 2016, Mayo conceded two own goals against Dublin, forcing a draw and a replay, which it lost.

The last of these finals, in 2021, came a few weeks before the final playing member of the original team, Paddy Prendergast, died aged 95.

The team did not make it back to Croke Park for the All-Ireland final until Sunday's decider against defending champions Kerry, who were trying to extend their record by winning a 40th All-Ireland crown.

So this year was the first opportunity to win the biggest game of the season since the elements of the "curse" had been met.

Things did not start well, with Kerry superstar forward David Clifford burying a shot in the net in the 15th minute.

But Mayo fought back to be a point down at half-time, 1-8 (11) to 0-10 (10).

Manager Andy Moran had backed young talent, with 18-year-old Kobe McDonald and 19-year-old Darragh Beirne key to the team's success.

McDonald, who was selected by St Kilda late last year as a Category B rookie and is expected to head Down Under shortly to join the team, would score three points in the final

Beirne's brilliant finish scored Mayo's only goal that sparked the county's run to victory.

Rollercoaster ride to All-Ireland title for Mayo

It had not been an auspicious start to the football season for Mayo, as it was beaten by 10 points by Roscommon in the Connacht provincial championship. The team in red and green was all but written off for the All-Ireland.

Andy Moran (right) got stuck into the media for laughing at long-suffering fans' celebrations. (Getty Images: Sportsfile/Ramsey Cardy)

It entered the All-Ireland Championship series still looking shaky, beating Monaghan by a point before a single-point loss to Tyrone left it on its final chance.

Mayo bounced back with a win over Meath to reach the quarter-finals, then downed Cork at Croke Park to make the last four.

The semi-final turned out to be a one-sided affair against Louth, with Mayo winning by 17 points. But the run was expected to end against Kerry. The questions started after the semi, with Moran asked if fans would lose the run of themselves celebrating given the county's horror record in finals.

Moran hit back hard.

"You laugh at that, lads. I don't laugh at that," Moran said at the press conference.

"I find it very, actually, dismissive, if I'm being honest. I think it's a bullshit question. I think it's a disrespectful question.

"Our county has been starved the last four or five years. If they [fans] go a bit nuts, let them."

He then set his sights on the football reporters present.

"You're going to go to a game tomorrow. Every single one of ye, you're going to write that Kerry or Dublin will go to win the All-Ireland final, right? Right?

"Does anyone here think we're going to win the All-Ireland final? No. Thank you."

Kobe McDonald has just finished school, but the Mayo young gun now has an All-Ireland medal and is set to come to the AFL. (Getty Images: Sportsfile/David Fitzgerald)

When the final siren went on Sunday, it set off emotional scenes at Croke Park among the 80,000-plus crowd.

The Saw Doctors' hit The Green and Red of Mayo, written by a group of Galway musicians about what Mayo means to the people, blasted out of the speakers at the stadium as joy mixed with disbelief for the fans.

After the game, McDonald, like his teammates, was elated and he was trying to focus on the now, rather than what's next.

"Look, to be honest I'm not thinking about Australia right now. I'm just going to soak in every minute of this. To give the people of Mayo something to celebrate, it's special," he told Irish broadcaster RTE.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"I know every team probably says it but we're like a family. When we're in training three days a week it's like 40 brothers.

"We know every single person in there has each other's back and whatever is being said outside the group doesn't affect us."

Gaelic games, football and hurling, are amateur sports, and there has been plenty of debate over the years about the loss of talent to the AFL.

The rest of Mayo, and quite possibly the rest of Irish Gaelic games, hopes that McDonald stays with Mayo and doesn't take his skills to Australia.

But whatever happens from here, McDonald and the rest of the team have written their names in Irish sporting history and moved their county forever beyond the ghosts of losses past.

A huge crowd of Mayo supporters travelled to Dublin and were overjoyed after their team's shock win. (Getty Images: Sportsfile/David Fitzgerald)

title: Scottish-blooded Anderson thrilled to win gold in Glasgow instead of Victoria
text:
There are a lot of Australians bemoaning the 2026 Commonwealth Games being held in Glasgow instead of regional Victoria, but don't make the mistake of thinking Iona Anderson is one of them.

Anderson emerged as Australia's biggest backstroke star of these Games when undisputed queen Kaylee McKeown withdrew due to glandular fever.

In the 200m, she finished sixth, over two seconds slower than the time she swam at the Australian trials in June.

But in the 100m, she touched first and it could not have been a better place for her first individual gold medal at a senior meet, storming past Canadian veteran and nine-time Commonwealth medallist Kylie Masse.

360 moment for Vicky Belando Nicholson Victoria Belando Nicholson was a baby when she was pulled lifeless from the water after falling from a refugee boat. Now she's a swimming bronze medallist for Australia.

Anderson got it done in the home of her forebears, if not herself, welcoming the controversial late change to the Scottish capital.

"Personally, for me, I think Glasgow's better than Victoria. Sorry," she laughed.

"I love the Scottish. I've got quite a few friends here and obviously my family. So it was great to come back here and do it."

Basically her entire family is from Scotland, Grangemouth on her mum's side and Dumfries and Galloway on her dad's.

Anderson was even named after the small island of Iona off the west coast of the country.

As she took her victory lap, the 20-year-old found her grandma Pam, who had been riding every drop of water displaced by Anderson's furious charge home.

"She was pretty emotional, there wasn't many words," she said.

"She's just really happy and stoked for me. She's always messaging me and always giving me good luck wishes, so that was really special to see her after the race."

The victory was comfortably the tightest of the night by any of the Australian swimmers as the Dolphins took home five more golds and 14 medals in total.

Cam McEvoy completed the full set of 50m freestyle titles by adding Commonwealth gold to Olympic and world titles, baton bearer Tim Hodge enjoyed another moment in the sun with gold in the 100m backstroke S9, Kai Taylor swam a glorious final leg to win the men's 4x200m relay, and Lani Pallister romped home in the women's 1,500m final for her second gold of the Games with the 200m and 800m to come.

Her victory gap of almost 18 seconds was 299 times bigger than Anderson's 0.06 margin over Masse.

A teenage Iona Anderson finished fifth as Kaylee McKeown completed the third leg of her double-double in Paris. (Getty Images: Maddie Meyer)

"I kept my blinders on so I'm really happy I got my hand on the wall," Anderson said.

"I could see some splashes, but to be honest, I closed my eyes at the end and hoped for the best."

The difficulty for Anderson is the spectre of McKeown.

The 25-year-old's double-double – winning the 100m and 200m backstroke at successive Olympics – has raised the bar for how greatness is defined in that discipline for the entire swimming world.

Perhaps that is why Anderson's distant finish in the longer race did not stay with her too long.

"I know I'm capable of more in the 200m but I've got to take away the positive that that's my third best swim ever," she said.

"I really just picked myself up and moved on."

title: AFL confirms State of Origin future with Victoria left out of 2027 game
text:
The AFL has confirmed the future of State of Origin, with Western Australia to host South Australia in 2027.

South Australia will then host Victoria in 2028 at Adelaide Oval, before Victoria and Western Australia meet again in Perth in 2029.

The State of Origin concept returned to the AFL in 2026, with Victoria beating Western Australia at a sold out Perth Stadium.

South Australia and Western Australia last played each other in 1998 at Football Park, with South Australia winning by 36 points in front of 18,000 fans.

AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon said the success of Origin's return earlier this year showed the event could go on to get bigger and better.

Trent Rivers of Western Australia kicks the ball during this year's AFL Origin match at Perth Stadium. (AAP Image: Richard Wainwright)

"No one really knew what the game was going to be like, and what we saw was actually footy at its finest, the ball moved around … it was a quick game, lots of scoring, so I think what we'll see is there'll be a different build-up for the players," he said.

"State football is one of the great traditions of our game, and we are pleased to see it continue in 2027 and beyond after the huge success of its return earlier this year which saw more than 58,000 people fill [Perth] Stadium in Perth.

Andrew Dillon says the success of February's WA-Victoria clash shows the concept has a future. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)



"Origin inspires passion, state pride and draws upon decades of rivalries that are central to the history of our game and our greatest players." "Origin inspires passion, state pride and draws upon decades of rivalries that are central to the history of our game and our greatest players."

"Locking in the structure for the next three years provides fans, clubs, players and stakeholders certainty on Origin, allowing them to embrace the state rivalry and celebrate our great game."

WA ready to resume SA rivalry

WA Origin chair of selectors and former player Glen Jakovich said the state had a similarly strong rivalry with South Australia as there was with Victoria.

"Same reason, they think they're better than us," Jakovich said.

"The South Australians, they don't leave the welcome mat out for you, so I've got to return the favour.

"I've got up to six or seven months to start planning the demise of South Australia."

West Coast Eagles great Glen Jakovich is parochial when it comes to State of Origin football. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

Jakovich said this year's clash with Victoria had showed just how much it meant to the players to represent their states.

"Led by Patrick Cripps … at his age, two Brownlow Medals, achieved a lot in football, and he put it right up there as one of the pinnacles of his career," he said.

"He led the state with such great honour, so I look forward to that happening again. It's a great privilege."

Political football

WA Premier Roger Cook has challenged his South Australian counterpart Peter Malinauskas to a bet on the outcome of next year's game.

"I reckon the loser needs to provide a carton of quality beer from their state to the other, so I'm very much looking forward to getting a carton … from Mali any day after the match," he said.

Roger Cook wants to put a friendly wager on the outcome of the game. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

No other states have been marked to play in the Origin series, with the Allies concept — Tasmania, New South Wales, Queensland, ACT, and Northern Territory merged together — last used in 1998.

New South Wales joined with ACT and Queensland joined with the Northern Territory in 1993, with Tasmania fielding a standalone team.

title: Remote Indigenous community's only drug and alcohol rehab centre closes
text:
The only alcohol and drug rehabilitation centre in the remote Indigenous community of Woorabinda has closed after 14 years in operation.

Mimosa Creek Healing Centre, which opened in 2012 in the community south-west of Rockhampton, was run by not-for-profit organisation Central Queensland Indigenous Development (CQID).

It offered residential rehabilitation for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander men recovering from drug and alcohol abuse, among other community services.

In March, during a trustee meeting, the Woorabinda Aboriginal Shire Council opted to terminate CQID's lease for the centre.

Minutes from that meeting show the decision, a result of a tied vote, was based on community sentiment that reflected "genuine concern".

"Community members had expressed that the service, as currently delivered, was not culturally appropriate for Aboriginal men and that this was preventing men in the community from accessing support when experiencing difficulties with alcohol and other drugs," the minutes read.

"It was further noted the outcomes achieved by the service did not demonstrate the improvements expected. Community concern had been raised that participants were continuing to pass through the service without achieving rehabilitation or sustained recovery outcomes."

In March during a trustee meeting, the Woorabinda Aboriginal Shire Council opted to terminate CQID's lease for the centre. (ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly)

CQID chief executive Jason Field said details of the concerns, outside of the publicly available council minutes, had not been raised with the not-for-profit.

The organisation had successfully sought government funding in 2011 to build the facility, as well as deliver its associated programs.

Mr Field said although CQID had successfully locked in future funding for operations, the council told the team to vacate the premises by July 8.

He said CQID had requested two meetings with the council and had sent four letters, "pleading for the decision to be reviewed or overturned".

"This has been disregarded," Mr Field said.

Woorabinda Aboriginal Shire Council has been contacted for comment.

Woorabinda, an Indigenous community south-west of Rockhampton, has a population of about 1,000 people. (ABC Capricornia: Rachel McGhee)

CQID has found another location in Woorabinda to continue its other programs, including drug and alcohol services, family support, youth support and foster and kinship care services.

There is no set opening date for the new facility.

However, it will not be able to continue with residential rehabilitation because it does not have a fit-for-purpose location available.

CQID said it had not been told of any new plans for the Mimosa Creek Healing Centre building.

Last year, the council voted to adopt a new five-year Community Safety Plan, including a proposal to slowly introduce alcohol back into the community, after it was banned for 17 years.

The plan mentioned, "counselling, rehabilitation, and harm-reduction programs must be integrated into the strategy to address root causes of alcohol misuse".

It is not known if any existing alcohol restrictions have yet been eased.

title: Tree planting project creates jobs for future in Tennant Creek
text:
In a warm greenhouse in Tennant Creek, Warumungu woman Shauna Graham pats down soil at the base of a seedling in a pot.

The young, spindly plant will soon be ready to put down roots and grow on mining land a few kilometres away, as part of a tree planting rehabilitation project.

Shauna Graham says working makes her feel happy and proud. (ABC Alice Springs: Victoria Ellis)

While Ms Graham has been nurturing the plant to grow, a feeling has been blooming inside herself.

"It makes me feel happy and proud of myself," she said.

Red gums and morning glory are among the plants being trialled at the mine rehabilitation site. (ABC Alice Springs: Victoria Ellis)

The traditional owner said the rehabilitation site was right next to her country.

"It makes me, like, safe, close at home, you know? Building things out there and making plans out there, growing for the future."

Partnering for shared knowledge

Ms Graham is one of a handful of Indigenous Tennant Creek residents to be employed by Julalikari Council Aboriginal Corporation, which is contracted by Tennant Mines to plant trees as part of rehabilitation works at Tennant Mine's recently reopened Nobles Nob mine.

Julalikari chief executive Lachlan Wilkins said she would not be the last.

"Tennant Mines shares Julalikari's commitment to creating opportunities for Aboriginal people to access jobs in the mining industry," he said.

Lachlan Wilkins says the program is creating jobs and healing country. (ABC Alice Springs: Victoria Ellis)

"The partnership makes sense in that it creates job opportunities for local people, it helps heal country and it helps ensure that Tennant Mines is meeting its obligations to the traditional owners but also to its regulators."

The current contract covers a six-week trial to see which plant species will grow best at the mine site, but a Tennant Mines spokesperson said the partnership would "extend over the long-term" and was "critical" to ensure sustainable operations.

Tennant Mining says its partnership with Julalikari is critical for its sustainable operations. (ABC Alice Springs: Victoria Ellis)

"Through this partnership, we are building shared knowledge in how to conduct leading practice rehabilitation in the Barkly," the spokesperson said.

"At the moment, planting is focused in and around the Nobles operation, but it will be extended as our shared knowledge grows."

Working for change

Mr Wilkins said he hoped the partnership would create lasting change by improving employment rates in Tennant Creek.

"It creates an opportunity for people to get into meaningful jobs in an industry that's growing and it's got a long-term commitment here," he said.

"We love that because kids see their mum and dad or their brother and sister get to work and instead of them engaging in training just for the sake of training. They will see [them] go into a job and then there's a meaningful pathway.

"That's what we're really excited to try and support."

Shauna Graham with Julalikari's Janine Andrews, who has been supporting the tree planting project. (ABC Alice Springs: Victoria Ellis)

Ms Graham said while some people would not take up the work, she was determined to involve her family.

"Next time I go out there I'm going to show my grandchildren, my sons and daughters, yeah, to keep that for them in future," she said.

title: More action needed to protect female tradies from 'nasty sexism', experts say
text:
Standing in a stainless-steel boning room, working through a bucket of slimy chicken carcasses, Kirsten Drinkwater wouldn't want to be anywhere else.

The 19-year-old is following in the footsteps of her grandfather, who also worked in the local butcher in her regional Queensland hometown of Eidsvold, 400km north-west of Brisbane.

"He really inspired me, he got me into it," she said.

"He's very, very proud of me."

Kirsten Drinkwater is following in her grandfather's footsteps by working in the butcher in Eidsvold, in Queensland's North Burnett region. (ABC Wide Bay: James C Taylor)

A second-year butcher's apprentice, Ms Drinkwater is one of a growing number of Queensland women taking up the meat cleaver in this traditionally male-dominated role.

In Queensland, 35 women started a butcher's apprenticeship last year, 10 more than in 2022.

In fact, the number of female apprentice butchers in Queensland has more than tripled since 2020, according to the National Centre for Vocational Education Research, a non-profit that analyses vocational training statistics.

It's a trend seen across other trades, including plumbers, electricians and "fridgies" — refrigeration and air-conditioning mechanics.

Conversely, numbers are dropping in traditionally female roles, with nearly 200 fewer women starting a hairdressing apprenticeship in the same time.

Ms Drinkwater said changing cultural attitudes were behind the movement of women into majority-male trades.

"I just think it's becoming more accessible for us," she said.

"There's a lot less fear of being discriminated against … I can just feel it, something is happening and the world's just becoming a little bit more inclusive."

Tamika Banks won the apprentice of the year award at the 2026 Australian Meat Excellence Awards. (Supplied)

Low completions

Sarojni Choy is a researcher in adult vocational education at Griffith University, specialising in the challenges faced by female apprentices.

Professor Choy said improved public messaging and increasing numbers of role models were drawing more women to the trades, but more support was needed to help female apprentices complete their qualifications.

Of the 25 women who started a four-year butcher's apprenticeship in 2022, only 10 completed in 2025, while some sectors had produced no female tradespeople in recent years.

"I think we are seeing a real, if modest, shift towards some of the non-traditional occupations for women," Professor Choy said.

"The challenge now is to convert that interest into sustained participation and completion."

Rae Cooper says more action is needed to attract women to a greater range of industries with national skills shortages. (ABC News: Geoff Kemp)

The challenges faced by female apprentices can extend to serious sexual discrimination and harassment.

Rae Cooper is director of the Australian Centre for Gender Equality and Inclusion at Work at the University of Sydney.

She led a research project that found 25 per cent of women working in automotive trades had directly experienced sexual harassment at work.

"Everyday sexism, or actually pretty nasty sexism, we find are an experience of lots of women apprentices," Professor Cooper said.

In 2022, the federal parliament passed laws requiring employers to take proactive steps to end workplace sex discrimination and harassment.

Protesters at 2021 March 4 Justice rallies demanded an overhaul of sex discrimination legislation. (Abubakr Mahmoud (ABC))

Professor Cooper said while these new laws had brought a positive change to many workplaces, "some aren't taking it seriously enough".

A lack of support through pregnancy and child care is also forcing women out of the trades.

"When you interview women tradies, they'll often talk about the advice they give to younger apprentices, which is, 'Try not to get pregnant during the period of your apprenticeship,'" Professor Cooper said.

Broader funding needed

Federal government programs are supporting and incentivising increased female workforce participation.

Since early 2025, the federal government's Building Women's Careers Program has awarded $54.5 million towards driving cultural change that is more welcoming to women.

Ms Drinkwater says a changing culture of more inclusive workplaces is behind growing numbers of women entering male-dominated industries. (ABC Wide Bay: James C Taylor)

However, the scope of the program is limited to construction, clean energy, advanced manufacturing, and digital and technology industries.

Professor Cooper said more needed to be done to attract women to a greater range of industries with national skills shortages.

A spokesperson for the federal Department of Employment and Workplace Relations said women accounted for most free TAFE enrolments, and that apprentices and their employers in priority industries may be eligible for additional grants and incentives.

New attitudes in the next generation

Professor Cooper said changing attitudes among younger workers were also driving cultural change.

"I think that the next generation of people who are commencing apprenticeships, particularly the young women, is less likely to put up with some of the things that women of their mothers' generation might have put up with," she said.

"And I think that's a good thing."

Following her apprenticeship Kirsten Drinkwater plans to travel to Germany and Spain to learn about the small goods trade in those countries. (ABC Wide Bay: James C Taylor)

Ms Drinkwater advised any girls seeking to follow in her footsteps to do their research when choosing an employer.

"It can be difficult to find a workplace where you're accepted," she said.

"But once you find the perfect spot, it's pretty easy to settle down and just get into it."

title: Hotel 'crisis' looms for thousands of travellers landing at new airport
text:
The lack of hotels near the soon-to-be-opened Western Sydney Airport (WSI) has been flagged as a major issue that could potentially impact the initial economic benefits of the new airport.

Due to open to passenger flights on October 25, operational trials at one of Australia's only 24/7 airports have been taking place, with cargo services set to officially start today.

Adam Leto, chief executive of Western Sydney Leadership Dialogue, said the area badly needed more hotels.

"We have got thousands of visitors landing on our doorstep starting from the end of this year that are going to be looking to stay, play and spend time in Western Sydney," he said.

"And we want to be able to keep them here, not have them move across the city for accommodation."

Mr Leto says more hotels are needed in the area to accommodate the numbers of projected passengers. (Supplied)

He said there were some new hotels in the pipeline near WSI, as well as in Parramatta, some 40 kilometres away.

Currently, there are only a handful of hotels within a 20km radius of the airport.

"There is no denying we have a hotel crisis at the moment. The state government has recognised there is a shortfall of beds in Western Sydney."

A spokesperson for the planned 200-room Courtyard by Marriott hotel, set to be built near the airport, said "there is not an opening timeline to share at this stage".

Do you know more? If you have any information about the story, contact Danuta Kozaki.

Established hotels set to benefit

Lauren Raffen is the owner and licensee of one of the hotels closest to the airport, the Wallacia Hotel.

While her hotel is set to benefit from the influx of travellers, she is concerned Western Sydney will not be able to accommodate the projected numbers.

"There's not too much around for the travellers coming in," she said.

"I don't know how we're going to keep them out here because there is not enough [hotels]."

Ms Raffen is also concerned about the lack of facilities locally for travellers. (ABC News: Adam Griffiths)

She said there was great anticipation ahead of passenger flights in and out of WSI

"There is a lot of excitement here in Wallacia, reservations too because of the aircraft noise," she said.

"But a lot of the locals are excited, and business owners are too because it's going to bring in a lot of people."

The historic hotel is 14km west of the new airport and has 29 rooms with ensuites.

According to the Wallacia Progress Association's website, the 1930s hotel was requisitioned by the army during World War II.

"During the Second World War the hotel was used as the Army headquarters for radiophysics," it said.

The Wallacia Hotel is 14 kilometres west of the new airport. (ABC News: Adam Griffiths)

With little public transport in the area, Ms Raffen said the hotel had plans to help passengers who have made reservations.

" We are putting a courtesy bus in place to make it convenient for travellers to and from the airport. "

She said the hotel, including its bistro and bar, already had many visitors from all over Sydney and the state on the weekends. There had also already been requests ahead of the airport's opening, especially from regional NSW.

"A lot of people from the state's Central West have said they will drive down and either stay the night before travelling if they have an early flight, or people planning to come in late at night have asked about staying here."

Mr Leto said other hotels in nearby Liverpool, Penrith and Rooty Hill were also expected to benefit.

Construction costs and red tape

Adding to the lag in new hotels, Mr Leto said, has been the cost of construction across Sydney.

"The market conditions, particularly when it comes to costs, whether you are talking residential or new hotels, the cost of construction across the city, particularly Western Sydney is challenging at the moment."

The cost of construction has been blamed as one of the reasons behind the lag in new hotel builds. (ABC News: Adam Griffiths)

He added that red tape and the unknown were also factors.

"The market is also a little hesitant and not quite sure what the demand is going to look like," he said.

"But as soon as the planes start touching down and we start to see the numbers rolling in, I am expecting that will spur a bit more confidence."

A spokesperson for WSI said it expected private sector investment to increase.

"We fully expect that the private sector will respond to this demand as it develops," they said.

"WSI has already been the catalyst for billions of dollars in broader infrastructure in the Western Sydney Aerotropolis, supporting road networks, and beyond."

A spokesperson for the airport says "the private sector will respond to this demand". (ABC News: Adam Griffiths)

Look to the future

The spokesperson for WSI said business was expected to grow.

New airport's neighbours feel overlooked Luddenham is a five-minute drive from Western Sydney International Airport, but some residents say they are missing out on the benefits it should be bringing them.m.

"Western Sydney International is built to meet demand for decades to come and will drive growth for the NSW visitor economy well into the future," they said.

"The airport is currently built to service 10 million passengers annually and will grow to service more than 80 million by the 2060s."

Mr Leto said it would become a major economic centre for Western Sydney over the next decade.

"It is going to take some time, like the broader picture around the Aerotropolis. You know Rome wasn't built in one day."

title: An orange wave is breaking over Victoria. Can Labor hold back the populist tide?
text:
No matter who emerges from Labor’s leadership contest, the victor will have to prepare to fight One Nation. This feature has been republished in the wake of Jacinta Allan’s colleagues turning against her.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The hard men and women of the union movement gathered at a conference centre on the edge of Melbourne didn’t entirely believe what they were being told. Kos Samaras, a former Labor Party organiser turned pollster and political consultant, was on his feet, explaining how One Nation, a party which had never won a lower house seat in Victoria, was on track to snatch a dozen at the next state election. In some Labor-held electorates, Pauline Hanson’s lot was Hoovering up 30 per cent of the vote. The room was not entirely convinced. Any union secretary worth their salt knows the mood on the factory floor, in the smoko room, around the teachers’ staff room. They weren’t picking up what Samaras was telling them. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson at a fundraiser in Melbourne on Friday night. Simon Schluter As it turns out, they were right to be sceptical. Samaras didn’t know the half of it. The setting was the annual strategic forum of Victorian Trades Hall Council, the state’s peak body for trade unions, at a venue in Chirnside Park. The date was March, after One Nation had flexed in South Australia, but before Hanson’s party reduced the Liberal and National parties to bit players in the Farrer byelection. What seemed an alarming prediction now appears a gross underestimation of where One Nation is heading. “People thought that 12 seats was maybe a stretch,” Trades Hall secretary Luke Hilakari recalls of the forum. “Now I’m looking at numbers like it could be 30 seats.”

Advertisement

Follow live updates: Jacinta Allan faces leadership threat To put this into context, the Liberal and National parties currently hold 29 seats in Victoria’s Legislative Assembly (lower house). If the revised projections commissioned by Trades Hall are accurate, One Nation will in November become the second-largest party in parliament behind Labor, and the dominant coalition partner within any non-Labor government. As dramatic as this outcome would be, it is only part of the seismic shift we are seeing in Victoria, one mirrored in Donald Trump’s America, in Nigel Farage’s UK and across Western Europe, where populist movements have either replaced or decimated traditional centre-right parties. Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election One Nation entrenched as third force as Victorians adopt ‘drain the swamp’ mentality The Victorian election, the first since One Nation overtook both major parties in popularity, could also produce the next step in Australia’s political upheaval – the emergence of an anti-establishment force capable of taking ground from both the right and the left, and muscling its way onto the government benches. Jim Reed, founder of the Resolve Political Monitor surveys published by The Age, says One Nation has morphed from a protest movement into an agent of change that voters from a broad range of demographics are approaching with positive intent. “The polls are showing One Nation stealing votes from both major parties, not just the right,” he says. Reed’s next survey of Victorian voting intentions will be published on Monday.

Advertisement

Federal One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce declared to 3AW on Friday that his party was now a force that both sides of politics needed to reckon with. “The movement’s on. It’s not an aberration,” he said. When seen this way, the November 28 poll is less a contest between Labor and Liberal than an insider-outsider stoush in which Labor’s biggest fight is against One Nation, the Coalition’s greatest rival is One Nation, and the make-up of parliament will be decided by a kaleidoscope of contests – red versus blue versus orange, not to mention green and teal. Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election Jacinta Allan vows to take up fight against ‘anti-worker’ One Nation A Labor versus Liberal fight for a marginal, mortgage belt seat will seem almost quaint. Back in March, the union leaders left Chirnside Park with another piece of work commissioned by Trades Hall: a 67-page thesis developed by a clever young researcher named Oscar Kaspi-Crutchett, about how the left should fight the far right. Simply titled Antidote, it presents the case that while right-wing populism often begins as a glitch in the centre-right matrix, its “path to power leads through the working class”. This is where the broader labour movement, including the Victorian ALP and the Allan government, wants to take the fight ahead of the election. While the Spring Street echo chamber is preoccupied with speculation about a challenge to Jacinta Allan’s leadership, Hilakari knows Labor faces far bigger questions.

Advertisement

“This is the most progressive state in the nation,” he says. “If One Nation plants their flag here in Victoria, they’re every chance to sweep the nation. This is where the fight is. This is the battleground. If we can’t push them out of Victoria, what’s that going to be like for Queensland, NSW and then the federal election? “We’re running against Pauline Hanson.” Allan this week sought to reframe the contest and sharpen her party’s focus and response to One Nation’s electoral threat. On a crisp winter’s day, she found an hour to slip out of her Treasury Place office, walk with this masthead around Fitzroy Gardens, and share her thoughts about what we are seeing in national and Victorian politics. “What we knew as the old rules of politics don’t exist,” Allan says. “What we are seeing here with the fracturing of mainstream political parties is happening in Victoria, around the country and other parts of the world. Victorian Premier Jacinta Allan says One Nation’s policies will hurt the same working people drawn to its cause. Justin McManus “We are the next big election going around. South Australia was an indicator, and obviously in published polls at a national level and state level around the country, we are seeing the One Nation vote surge. I think One Nation are a risk to working people and families everywhere, and we are the next ones who will be going up against them. That is why you will see me talk a lot about job security, about supporting workers, about helping people.” Allan has raised the spectre of a One Nation-Liberal government. Under this scenario, Hanson, a Queensland senator but with the ultimate authority within One Nation, would have a real and present influence over Victoria’s affairs. Invert the question of how Opposition Leader Jess Wilson would govern if she accepts One Nation as a junior Coalition partner. What would One Nation’s Victorian leader – a position yet to be filled– do as premier?

Advertisement

Either way, the election will break new ground. This is the first state or federal election since One Nation’s revival a decade ago where it is poised to win seats from Labor as well as the Coalition. This didn’t happen in South Australia, where One Nation won four lower house seats off the Liberal Party. It didn’t happen in Farrer, where Labor didn’t contest, and One Nation won a federal seat held by the Coalition since its creation. To find the last time it did, you need to go back to 1998, when the first iteration of One Nation won six seats from Labor and five from the Nationals at the Queensland state election. Hanson says her ultimate aim in Victoria is to remove a long-term Labor administration that has plunged the state into record debt, allowed criminals to infiltrate its Big Build program and overseen record levels of crime. She told a fundraiser event in Melbourne on Friday night she would be willing to partner the Coalition in government to achieve this goal. While opinion is split about whether this is a gift to the Liberal Party or a curse, Allan is clear on what the worst outcome would be: a One Nation-led government. Loading The Liberal Party will, meanwhile, keep pressing the case that if One Nation supporters really want to change the government, the best way is to vote for the Coalition. To understand what the next parliament could look like, let’s return to the Redbridge seat-by-seat modelling Samaras presented to the Trades Hall Council in March, and has since updated. It showed Labor’s seats most likely to be swamped by an orange wave are in outer suburban and semi-rural areas, like Melton and Sydenham in Melbourne’s west and Pakenham, Bass and Hastings in the south-east. These are areas on the front line of the population debate that Hanson has sought to exploit as she blames “mass immigration” for overburdened roads, trains, schools and hospitals.

Advertisement

They also have a higher proportion of people who are not university educated and who are either production workers, service workers or small business owners. Kaspi-Crutchett identifies these three groups as having changeable political allegiances. “These communities are more exposed to economic shocks and consequently exhibit outsized discontent with the status quo,” he says in Antidote. Wherever the far-right has achieved critical mass, it has done so by winning over significant portions of these occupational groups, Kaspi-Crutchett says. The urban fringe is also a dangerous place for the Liberal Party, with similar seats, such as Berwick (the electorate held by former leader Brad Battin), Croydon and Evelyn (which includes Chirnside Park) also in play. The electoral map for the Nationals is even more bleak because One Nation was already resonating with some regional voters at the 2022 state election. Samaras’ research shows seats such as Murray Plains, Gippsland East, Shepparton and Euroa are at risk of turning orange. Samaras, who declined to discuss his confidential modelling, says that on published polling results, the Nationals could lose all their seats. But he adds an important caveat: “If you were going to pick a group of National MPs who could defend their seats because of who they are, I would pick the Victorians.” Nationals leader Danny O’Brien says that at the last election, voters elected four new National MPs, including two who replaced independents. “Our great party has been written off many times in our 110-year history, but we have always prevailed because country people want a party that looks out for them and fights for their fair share,” he says. Publican Andrew Lethlean is trying to win Jacinta Allan’s seat of Bendigo East for the Nationals this November. Penny Stephens The nuclear scenario, one canvassed by a Labor source, is that One Nation could wipe all established parties off Victoria’s regional and rural map. Speaking on the condition of anonymity, the source said the outlook for Labor had deteriorated from bad to catastrophic. If this situation is realised, then Allan’s seat of Bendigo East is squarely in the One Nation firing line. This comes on top of a well-planned Nationals challenge by Andrew Lethlean, a publican who took Labor’s overlapping federal seat of Bendigo to the brink of defeat in last year’s federal election. On the desk of his Trades Hall office, Hilakari has an electoral map which, with each new input of data, he colours with shades of orange, blue, red and green. The state of Victoria already resembles a tequila sunset, with One Nation’s putative seats stretching from the edge of Melbourne to the NSW border. Trades Hall secretary Luke Hilakari. Simon Schluter There was a view among Labor, one expressed not long ago, that One Nation and the Liberals would devour one another, leaving the ALP as the only party capable of forming government. This has now been replaced by a growing sense of despair about what to do with a problem like Pauline. A frustrated party official says: “We have a woman who is backed by billionaires, who does not vote for increases in the minimum wage or the pension, who says that people are lazy and don’t want to work, and somehow she is the champion of the working class.” How Victoria – where Labor has governed for all but four years this century – arrived at this place is also a live debate. Kaspi-Crutchett traces the economic and social forces that tilled the soil for Hanson, such as the declining share of the economy paid to workers, growing disparities in the distribution of wealth, and the bleak outlook confronting younger Australians witnessing the disappearance of entry-level jobs and prohibitive house prices. An Essential poll published in the lead-up to the 2025 federal election suggests that even though Labor voters backed in the Albanese government, they weren’t in a good place. According to the survey, only 16 per cent of Labor voters believed the political system was working well, and most felt Australia was on the wrong track. Not many of them will put much weight on this story – only 11 per cent trusted the mainstream media to report accurately. Related Article Opinion

One Nation Like Trump, Hanson’s rise is beyond politics. That’s why she’ll be hard to stop Peter Hartcher Political and international editor Kaspi-Crutchett also presents some uniquely Victorian factors which help explain One Nation’s sudden appeal, noting the COVID-19 experience and particularly the 262 days Melbourne spent in lockdown “turbocharged both the scale and intensity of far-right political activity in the state”. Lydia Khalil and Joshua Roose, experts on extremism, described the anti-lockdown movement in a 2023 paper as “a wide array of actors, including anti-vaxxers, religious communities, wellness influencers, QAnon and other conspiracists, sovereign citizens, and known Australian far-right actors and influencers” who converged alongside ordinary citizens to protest against vaccine mandates and social restrictions. From this unlikely cluster of bedfellows, a cohesive movement formed. Labor knows it is both inaccurate and counterproductive to dismiss One Nation supporters as racist or conspiratorial cranks. Instead, the party’s state and federal headquarters are directing its MPs, including Allan, to shift the argument to what a Labor government can do for working people and what One Nation won’t. That shift has begun, but the hour is late. In a little over five months, Victorians go to the polls for one of the most consequential elections in the state’s history. At least Labor now knows who it is fighting. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. Sign up for our Morning Edition newsletter.

text:

Key points THEATRE: Melbourne Theatre Company’s Uncle Vanya offers up sardonic one-liners

MUSIC: ACO’s From Winter’s Stillness is an edgy musical hybrid

THEATRE

Uncle Vanya ★★★★

Melbourne Theatre Company, Arts Centre Melbourne, until August 22 It’s a rare and charming thing to see Uncle Vanya done in period dress, as it is in Anne-Louise Sarks’ latest production for the MTC, on a splendid set that evokes a crumbling provincial estate in the last decade of the 19th century. Singling out actors for praise in Chekhov may be inevitable but always feels like a betrayal. Pia Johnson Contemporary Chekhovian performance tends to modernise, reframe, relocate. It’s as if we wanted to fire a bullet at the past – an exercise in futility, as Vanya himself discovers twice. Time doesn’t work that way. Playwright Joanna Murray-Smith believes (rightly) that such modernising is unnecessary in a good Chekhov production. Her Vanya adaptation gives a light textual massage for clarity, to draw out the comedy and update the vernacular.

Advertisement

As you’d expect from Murray-Smith, the sardonic one-liners are mercilessly sharp, and characters slip in words like “f---wit” and “bonking”, while being aware enough to admit that, well, “No one says ‘bonking’ any more.” Beyond that and the sound design – the Violent Femmes’ Add It Up doesn’t feel appropriate to the general vibe – it’s a faithful, lightly periodised production and an excellent intro to Chekhovian tragicomedy. It’s a rare and charming thing to see Uncle Vanya done in period dress. Pia Johnson Singling out actors for praise in Chekhov may be inevitable but always feels like a betrayal. Star turns can damage the delicate ensemble performance required to portray human contingency and incompleteness, and on that level this production sometimes feels more like a collection of exquisitely rendered individual performances – the human equivalent of the autumn leaves falling in its opening scene – than a true ensemble piece. There’s still much to admire. Sarks emphasises humiliation as key to whatever self-awareness the characters might avoid or achieve, and the romantic excruciations (everyone is famously in love with the wrong person) are beautifully done.

Advertisement

Philippa Northeast invests the role of Sonya with girlish comedy, throwing herself at Astrov (Fayssal Bazzi) with the full cringe of unrequited infatuation, while the charismatic doctor and environmentalist – whose dashing good looks and vaulting idealism coexist with burnout and radical disillusionment and emotional disconnection – seduces the beautiful young Yelena (Catherine Văn-Davies) with a palpable edge of self-loathing. Daniel Henshall’s Vanya is a veritable humiliation magnet. It’s a notably unsympathetic portrayal. A beta male to the core, this Vanya is an intensely pathetic figure who projects his own inadequacies onto his brother-in-law, the Professor (played in a nimble, lightly drawn lampoon of intellectual pomposity by Shaun Micallef) even as he makes embarrassing moves on the Professor’s young wife and pours blatant misogyny over everyone, including his would-be suffragist mother (Carolyn Bock). Daniel Henshall’s Vanya is a veritable humiliation magnet. Pia Johnson Vanya might feel like a minor character in his own life, but it’s Chekhov’s actual minor characters who cope best with humiliation. The longsuffering Waffles (Don Bridges) is warmly and affectionately conveyed, as is the stolidity of the pipe-smoking Nanny (Evelyn Krape). They’re both gloriously unselfconscious – one antidote to humiliation – and such brief moments of freedom are among the production’s most elevating, including a poignant scene where Sonya and Yelena are together, chatting and drinking and playing together like sisters, away from all the fuss the men are causing.

Advertisement

On opening night, some performances didn’t seem entirely bedded down. Henshall appeared to go dry at one point – a metatheatrical humiliation that seemed apposite, in context – but it might be the consistency of dramatic tempo that’s the biggest niggle. Related Article Streaming It may offend the book’s rusted-on fans, but this series should be approached with an open mind How we experience time, and how we handle futility and ennui, are among Chekhov’s main themes, and the one time I saw the Russians perform Vanya – by the Maly Drama Theatre of St Petersburg in 2007 – they brazenly manipulated the elastic temporal quality of theatre. (That production went for over three hours, dared the audience to be bored, and unfolded as inescapably as if it were being performed inside a black hole.) It would be churlish – maybe even Vanya-like – to complain that the audience wasn’t bored enough, though, and if it doesn’t quite deliver the epiphany into the human condition you get from the highest level of Chekhovian performance, this production’s desire to entertain is a no less crucial element of the drama. After all, Chekhov’s characters are always performing to allay such tedium, or at least give it form. And that aspect of being human is as timeless as it gets.

Reviewed by Cameron Woodhead

Advertisement

MUSIC

From Winter’s Stillness ★★★★

Australian Chamber Orchestra, Hamer Hall, until July 27 What do you get when you cross the Australian Chamber Orchestra with a jazz trumpeter and a Norwegian trio of female voices specialising in medieval, Nordic folk and contemporary music? Trumpeter Arve Henriksen performs is performing with the Australian Chamber Orchestra. Julia Marie Naglestad Well, certainly an edgy musical hybrid pushing the boundaries of “classical” programming, delighting intrepid listeners and probably perplexing others. The perplexity was heightened because printed programs only became available at interval, leaving most of the audience adrift in the unusual musical terrain of the first half. Trumpeter Arve Henriksen’s The Plume of Ash and Acceptance set a reflective mood, contrasted by the indefatigable minimalism of Terry Riley’s Half Wolf Dances Mad in the Moonlight.

Advertisement

Estonian composer Tõnu Kõrvits’ Bells, written for Henriksen and Trio Mediæval (singers Anna Maria Friman, Ditte Marie Bræin and Jorunn Lovise Husan), exerted a mesmeric quality that sat well alongside Academy Award-winning Icelandic composer Hildur Guðnadóttir’s Time and Water (especially written for this tour). Related Article ★★★★★

Melbourne live reviews It took 48 years, but this show has finally made it to Melbourne. It was worth the wait This Little Child, a sad traditional Norwegian song preceded Icelandic band Sigur Ros’ Fljótavik, an ideal vehicle for Hendriksen, whose unique, mellow tone unfurled over the music’s ground bass. In the second half, movements of Soviet composer Alfred Schnittke’s Concerto Grosso No.1 were interleaved with jazz-infused musings on Nordic chant and folk material. Schnittke’s iconoclasm is mercifully leavened with a generous sense of humour. Soloists Richard Tognetti and Satu Vänskä met the outrageous technical demands with aplomb, aided by customarily fine support from the rest of the ACO.

Advertisement

Using a cyclorama against which performers were either silhouetted or spotlit, head of lighting Joe Cox created a welcoming, unifying mood across this diverse program. Trio Mediæval’s limpid vocal quality was a delight throughout and together with flashes of brilliance from Henriksen, this eclectic experience was bound to get listeners talking – presumably as the ACO intended.

Barkly Rare Earths has sent the first batch of samples from its 10,000-metre resource expansion drill campaign to the laboratory, a key step in its push to grow its already significant rare earths inventory at its flagship Barkly project in the Northern Territory. The campaign is designed to test for shallow mineralisation around the company’s existing 40-million-tonne inferred mineral resource, which grades an impressive 2100 parts per million (ppm) total rare earth oxides (TREO). Barkly Rare Earths Managing Director, Craig Wright, inspects laboratory sample preparation equipment at the ALS laboratory in Brisbane to be used for samples from the company’s 10,000m NT drilling campaign. Previous drilling between these two areas intersected rare earths hinting at the potential for significant lateral expansion across the intervening 20-kilometre corridor. Barkly has defined an exploration target that gives a sense of the scale it is chasing. It ranges from 200 million to 1 billion tonnes at a grade of between 1600 and 1900 ppm TREO. If the company can get anywhere near even the lower end of that range, it could potentially be sitting on a globally significant deposit.

Advertisement

‘This is where the campaign moves from metres drilled to assay results.’ Barkly Rare Earths managing director Craig Wright The company has adopted a two-pronged strategy for the campaign. The early stage will involve drilling a series of deeper, 60-metre holes to provide a stronger geological framework for the current deposit. The rig will then move on to the main event, a pattern of up to 400 shallow holes averaging just 25 metres deep targeting an area dubbed the Immediate Zone. This Immediate Zone sits within an underexplored 20-kilometre corridor connecting the two resource areas with the first samples from the program having already arrived at the ALS lab in Brisbane for analysis. Barkly Rare Earths managing director Craig Wright said: “The objective is clear, test the shallow mineralisation around our existing 40 Mt Inferred Resource and generate the data intended to support a resource update later this year.” Barkly says what makes the project compelling is not just the potential scale but the high proportion of valuable magnet rare earth oxides which account for 34 per cent of the total resource. These are the elements critical for manufacturing high-strength magnets used in everything from electric vehicles to wind turbines.

Advertisement

Critically, initial test work has yielded low levels of uranium and thorium – both unwanted elements which can often complicate processing. In another notable milestone leaching tests achieved a 74 per cent extraction rate for magnet rare earths with early-stage beneficiation work producing a mineral concentrate grading a hefty 29,000 ppm TREO. Additionally, Barkly is armed with two recent grants of $115,000 each awarded under the Northern Territory’s highly regarded Geophysics and Drilling Collaborations program. And while the company’s main game is its rare earths project, it also holds the Buntine project in the Northern Territory where it is chasing green fields base metals. Notably, it says the project’s geology at Buntine is the same as the rocks that host the world-class McArthur River lead-zinc deposit with polymetallic mineralisation already having been identified along a nine-kilometre strike length. Initial rock chipping has returned grades of up to one per cent lead, 1760 ppm cobalt and 7100 ppm nickel. In what looks to be a savvy business play, Barkly has farmed out the uranium rights at its Murphy West project, also in the NT, to fellow ASX-listed explorer DevEx Resources. The deal allows DevEx to earn up to a 75 per cent interest by spending $3.5 million over five years, giving Barkly an exploration “free kick” on its ground.

With the initial drill samples from its rare earths expansion campaign at the lab, the market will be watching for the first of the assay results to begin flowing shortly. Barkly has flagged its intentions to deliver a mineral resource updated during the final quarter of the year, and given the company is starting with 40 million tonnes in the bag, the company clearly has a huge exploration target in sight. And with plenty of prospective ground to test, things could soon get very interesting for Barkly as it looks to potentially define a project of global significance. For more than a quarter of a century, Asia’s best-known hotel food festival has unfolded beneath the chandeliers of one of Thailand’s grandest hotels. Sumba Food Festival’s Food Safari. Aacessible via a one-hour flight from Bali, Sumba has long been overshadowed by its famous neighbour. The remote Indonesian island receives only a fraction of Bali’s visitors, which makes it an unlikely setting for a gathering of eight of the Asia-Pacific’s leading chefs. Here, though, at the Sumba Food Festival, hosted by luxury eco-resort Cap Karoso, the destination – its produce, traditions and producers – is the primary ingredient. Guests head out on fishing boats at dawn, wander through the resort’s three-hectare organic farm, browse local markets alongside the chefs and later gather around communal tables to taste menus created from whatever Sumba has yielded that day.

The concept proved its worth when the festival debuted last year. Singapore chef Mano Thevar, whose restaurant Thevar holds two Michelin stars, became so captivated by the produce growing metres from the kitchen that he expanded his lunch menu after discovering banana, turmeric and galangal leaves harvested fresh from the farm. Cap Karoso, Sumba. Japanese chef Kanji Kobayashi, whose acclaimed Villa Aida is built around farming outside Osaka, admitted many of Sumba’s herbs and vegetables were unfamiliar. Cap Karoso founder Fabrice Ivara says such encounters are what the festival was created to encourage. Rather than flying chefs to Sumba simply to cook, he wanted them to spend time with local producers, discover unfamiliar ingredients and leave with a deeper understanding of the island’s culinary traditions.

Those discoveries have shaped this year’s program. Across two weeks, eight chefs from across the Asia-Pacific will each spend several days cooking, exploring and collaborating on the island. Among them are Seoul’s Joseph Lidgerwood, whose Evett holds two Michelin stars; Osaka’s Yusuke Takada of two-Michelin-starred La Cime; Bangkok duo Davide Garavaglia of Cote by Mauro Colagreco and Dan Bark of Cadence; Bali’s Gaetan Biesuz of Rumari at Raffles Bali; Indonesian locavore pioneer Eelke Plasmeijer of Locavore NXT in Ubud; Keiko Kuwakino of Japan’s mountain restaurant Sanaburi; and Brando Moros, the Michelin-starred chef behind Dubai’s 11 Woodfire. The format is intimate. Four-hands dinners, where two chefs collaborate on a one-off menu, are limited to just 22 guests. The wider program includes chef-led farm lunches, beach dinners and food safaris exploring Sumba’s varied landscapes. Related Article Indonesia Forget Bali. One of last year’s most memorable events wasn’t a Michelin-starred dinner at all, but a cooking competition for local home cooks. One entrant, aged more than 100, served a family chicken curry recipe that sent several visiting chefs home with fresh ideas. Proceeds from the festival help fund clean water projects, nutrition education, sustainable farming initiatives and grants for local food entrepreneurs working with Sumba’s native produce. Sumba is better known for its wild horses, ikat weaving, the Pasola Festival of spear-fighting, megalithic villages and rugged coastline. While not aiming to change that, the Sumba Food Festival adds another delicious dimension. The Sumba Food Festival runs October 5-18. See capkaroso.com
