Gateway Mining has again stretched the boundaries of its rapidly emerging Cowza gold discovery, adding another kilometre of high-grade strike to deliver an impressive 3.5-kilometre mineralised system at its Yandal gold project in Western Australia. The latest wide-spaced air-core drilling has confirmed strong continuity of gold mineralisation along every drill traverse completed to date, with standout intercepts including 4 metres grading 11.1 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 72m, 8m at 3.1g/t gold from 76m and 4m at 3.3g/t gold from 80m. Air-core drilling at Gateway Mining’s Yandal gold project in Western Australia, where ongoing drilling continues to expand the rapidly growing Cowza gold discovery. Barely a week after tripling the strike to 2.5 kilometres, Gateway has already pushed Cowza another kilometre farther, reinforcing the view that the discovery is still in rapid growth mode. Cowza’s strike is expanding almost as quickly as Gateway can drill it. Cowza sits on the contact between mafic and intermediate volcanic rocks within a 4.5km structural corridor showing strong demagnetisation, shearing and alteration – all classic hallmarks of a fertile gold system. Management believes the consistency of the geological signatures presents as a blueprint for further discoveries with the prospect of contacts and major regional shears repeatedly combining to host additional gold mineralisation across the project.

‘The growing body of evidence suggests Cowza has the potential to become a significant gold discovery within the Yandal Project.’ Gateway Mining chief executive officer Richard Pugh Adding to the intrigue, a further 1km of drilling north of the current assay area has already intersected the same favourable shearing, veining and alteration, suggesting the discovery could continue its march northwards. Assays for those holes are pending as Gateway continues testing extensions to the rapidly growing system. Gateway Mining chief executive officer Richard Pugh said: “The rapid growth of the Cowza system continues to exceed expectations, with gold mineralisation now defined over an impressive 3.5 kilometre strike length and remaining open in multiple directions.” Gateway is now stepping on the accelerator. A second reverse-circulation (RC) rig is arriving on site this week and will be dedicated entirely to Cowza as the company moves to define the rapidly expanding scale and continuity of the fresh-rock mineralisation. The first verdict on Heaps Normal’s first non-alcoholic sparkling wine Wine writer Katie Spain had High Hopes for the trailblazing beer brewers’ first foray into wine. So, how does it stack up upon tasting? Katie Spain July 27, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Stop press. I’ve got exciting news. We finally have an Australian-made non-alcoholic ‘wine’ that tastes like wine. Surprisingly, it took a beer brewer to nail it. I had high but cautious expectations when I caught wind that Sydney-based non-alc beer gurus Heaps Normal were releasing a High Hopes Prosecco. Since launching in July 2020, co-founder Ben Holdstock and his team raised the non-alc bar with their XPA, IPA, Lager, and Stout. But wine is a different beast. Heaps Normal have High Hopes for the new sparkling. Globally, few get it right, and the reason is simple. Alcohol literally brings a lot to the table. It provides mouthfeel and texture, palate weight, a warming sensation or heat, and psychological effects.

Advertisement

“When you take the ethanol out of wine, you lose a lot,” says Dr Wes Pearson, research scientist at the Australian Wine Research Institute (AWRI). The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up “Ethanol is a very unique compound, and there really isn’t much else like it chemically. When you remove that from wine, you’re left with something that is thin and acidic, has a watery feel and no longer resembles any concept of traditional wine.” So how did a self-proclaimed disruptive business with a non-alc beer background like Heaps Normal crack the code? Lots of research. Rage without alcohol with High Hopes. The sparkling wine took 18 months to develop, in collaboration with the Australian Wine Research Institute (AWRI), and is made with 100 per cent grapes sourced from Hilltops in NSW. Throughout the process, Heaps Normal head of wine, Ned Brooks, engaged with winemakers, bartenders and organic chemists at the AWRI’s No-Low Wine Research Centre.

Advertisement

“I did a bit of a deep dive into the category and tasted a lot,” Brooks says. “It always felt like people were making non-alcoholic wines just to fill a category in their range. There weren’t many who were actually trying to build a drink that was worthy of drinking.” While Australia has some impressive NoLo wine alternatives, the stuff made with grapes didn’t really cut it. Heaps Normal founders Andy Miller, Ben Holdstock and Peter Brennan. “In Australia, it felt like there was a method and no one really deviated from the method which was de-alkalise, add grape concentrate, add flavours, add colours, and add thickener,” Brooks says. “It seemed as if it was a bit of an easy answer, and no one was really willing to think outside the box and try and see what else they could come up with.”

Advertisement

There are some exceptions.



“Edenvale is exclusively a non-alcoholic wine producer, and there are a number of German, American and French producers that are exclusively non-alcoholic as well.” Edenvale is another non-alc prosecco maker. Dr Pearson said Heaps Normal’s approach to product development was “very clever”. “I think they have the benefit of creating products in this space without what I would almost call the ‘burden’ of having a wine background,” he says. “As a beer company, they aren’t obliged to make a product that is a replacement product for traditional wine, as their customers aren’t traditional wine drinkers. They just have to make a product that tastes good, and works for the occasions that their non-alc beer products are being consumed at.”

Advertisement

The wine is produced in-house. High Hopes is one out of the box. “In this instance, it was basically rethinking the whole process,” Brooks says. Not just the alkalization side, but even the harvest, the grape variety, when we’re picking [the grapes] and what we’re achieving in each step in the winemaking process, as opposed to it being an afterthought.” “I thought, ‘Can I make something that’s dry – kind of an aperitif style that’s going to suit somebody who wants to have it with oysters, rather than something that feels like sweet green bubbles?’” Ned Brooks, Heaps Normal head of wine Brooks’ wine background includes working in wineries, hospitality, retail and wholesale. He wanted to make something that worked as a standalone drink as well as with food.



“Prosecco as a category is so broad in the styles,” he says. “I thought, ‘Can I make something that’s dry – kind of an aperitif style that is going to suit somebody who wants to have it with oysters, rather than something that feels like sweet green bubbles?’”

Advertisement

As for what’s next for Heaps Normal, there are positive signs for those thirsty for a new, non-alc still wine option, too. “We’re currently working through the process of research and development on a still product”, says Brooks. “I don’t really have a date or anything like that, but we are trying to figure that out.” High Hopes from Heaps Normal The verdict My verdict on the Heaps Normal High Hopes Prosecco? It’s excellent. Smashing, even. It actually tastes like Prosecco. There are lashings of lemon, life-affirming fizz, head-snapping acidic twang, depth of flavour, and bubbles that last the distance.

A local upsizer paid $2 million for a small semi in Balmain after the vendor dropped their reserve by $100,000 at auction on Saturday. The two-bedder with stained glass, iron lacework, a leafy courtyard and upstairs balcony at 15 Gladstone Street had clear views across the city, including the Sydney Harbour Bridge. The property was one of 564 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney last week. By Saturday evening, Domain Group had recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 53 per cent from 311 reported results throughout the week, while 93 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. Three parties registered to bid on the Federation-era property with a $2 million guide. All were young couples or families, but only one made an offer, opening the auction at $1.9 million.

Advertisement

The next bid was a vendor bid of $2 million, then the opening bidder asked the auctioneer if they could match the vendor bid. This was accepted. Related Article Auctions First home buyers pay $2.04m for renovated Sydney house as market drops The vendor then agreed to adjust their reserve of $2.1 million, and it sold under the hammer for $2 million. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. Selling agent Richard Baini of Richard Matthews Real Estate said the street was full of onlookers: “The crowd was easily over 100 people.”

Advertisement

“There’s a lot more buyer confidence coming back into the market,” Baini said. “They’ve gone and reassessed their financial position with their brokers and banks, and the buyers are back out looking and buying again.” The vendor is moving out of Sydney. The house last traded for $463,000 in 1999, records show. In Dulwich Hill, a “shell” of a property in dire need of renovation sold for $840,000. The two-bedroom, top-floor apartment at 8/401 Marrickville Road drew four registrations. Three took part, and all were first home buyers.

Richardson & Wrench’s Aris Dendrinos noted uncertainty in the market. “It’s not a market of fear. It’s a market of uncertainty, and it’s the worst market because when people are fearful, they act. When they’re uncertain, they don’t act,” he said.

“People can panic buy, and people can panic sell because they’re fearful. They want to get their money. They want to move on and do the next thing. But when they’re uncertain, they don’t do much.” The deceased estate last traded for $158,000 in 1994, records show. In Sydney’s south-west, a three-bedroom property drew the interest of three builders who registered at auction. The Carramar block at 107 Mitchell Street was guided at $1 million. Bidding opened at $920,000 and went up in mostly $10,000 increments between the three active bidders.

When its reserve of $1.1 million was met, $2000 and $1000 bids proceeded back and forth until it sold for $45,000 above the reserve for $1,145,000. He said current zoning laws meant a granny flat was possible, but not a duplex. He also said that the buyer “may salvage the home and renovate it … if he can save it, he will. But if not, he’ll just knock it down and rebuild.” The address last traded for $99,000 in 1988, records show.

PRD chief economist Dr Diaswati Mardiasmo said Domain’s clearance rate of 53 per cent for Sydney is “a bit on the low side”. “I would imagine that’s probably because the law for SMSF and negative gearing and CGT was passed … sometimes it does take two, three weeks for it to translate through.” She said people are still figuring out what they want to do, what it means for them and their portfolio. “I know that Sydney has been really cold as well … but I think, more importantly, it’s just been a much lower market ever since the particular law has been passed when it comes to property taxes.”

title: Trump’s America is sinking as his war on the world sputters
text:
Advertisement

BusinessThe economyTrade wars Opinion Trump’s America is sinking as his war on the world sputters Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist July 27, 2026 — 11:59am

July 27, 2026 — 11:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Donald Trump keeps trying to build his tariff wall, but each time the wall is lower and built on narrower footings. When Trump announced his “Liberation Day” tariffs in April last year, they were expected to raise somewhere between $US1.5 trillion and $US2 trillion ($2.2 trillion to $2.9 trillion) over the next decade. Donald Trump has repeatedly sent conflicting signals about his plans for the Hormuz Strait. Getty Images Those tariffs, of course, got struck out by the US Supreme Court in February, forcing the Trump administration to come up with a replacement, which it did. As a temporary measure, using a section of the Trade Act with a ceiling rate of 15 per cent and forced expiry after 150 days, it imposed a 10 per cent duty on all imports that would raise about $US35 billion while it constructed a permanent replacement.

Advertisement

Those interim tariffs expired last Friday morning and were immediately replaced with a tariff of either 10 per cent or 12.5 per cent on 99.4 per cent of all goods imported to the US, other than those the administration explicitly excepted or where there is a different tariff regime in place, like the 50 per cent duty on imports of steel and aluminium. Related Article Trade As Trump’s new tariffs loom, Australian exporters clamour for carveouts The latest tariffs have supposedly been imposed because all of America’s trading partners, including Australia, have failed to sufficiently crack down on the use of forced labour. In reality, they are the latest attempt to recreate the revenue stream, and the barrier to imports, ruled illegal by the Supreme Court. Thanks to the Supreme Court, the revenue that was collected by the Liberation Day tariffs – more than $US160 billion – has to be refunded, though the administration has done what it can to slow the process and reduce the amount it must return. It has so far, however, paid back more than $US80 billion of the revenue it collected. Last month, the US government’s revenue from customs duties was negative to the tune of $US25.6 billion, after refunds virtually matched receipts in May.

Advertisement

Those tariffs that were supposed to be the interim measure while the administration developed its new permanent replacement for the one knocked out by the Supreme Court will have raised an estimated $US35 billion. The US Court of International Trade has, however, deemed those tariffs illegal too. If that ruling holds up under appeal, that revenue will also have to be refunded. America’s finances are parlous – and deteriorating. Bloomberg Some of the small businesses that successfully challenged the Liberation Day tariffs, and the lawyers who represented them, were involved in the action against the interim tariffs and have already filed a lawsuit against the new duty regime imposed last week. While the section of the Trade Act (Section 301) that the administration is using has been tried and tested and has held up in the courts previously, the sham pretext of inaction against forced labour being used to try to reproduce a global tariff regime to replace the one the Supreme Court declared illegal makes it vulnerable. Under the US Constitution, only Congress has the power to apply universal tariffs.

Advertisement

Related Article Opinion

Trump's White House Trump is back announcing a 2028 presidential bid. It’s not a joke Cory Alpert Former White House staffer Trump plans to use the same section of the Trade Act to impose even more tariffs, with the administration to argue that they are warranted in response to other nations’ trade measures that it deems discriminatory to American businesses. Even if the tariffs imposed last week do hold up under court scrutiny, they are – as revenue raisers – a poor substitute for the Liberation Day tariffs. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB) had a look at the new tariffs last week, along with other country-specific tariffs that Trump announced would be imposed on Canada and Brazil (apparently for their lack of deference to him). The CRFB estimated that the Supreme Court ruling would cost the US government about $US1.7 trillion of revenue it would otherwise have collected over the next decade.

Advertisement

The new universal tariffs, with a lower average rate and far more exclusions (to try to moderate their inflationary effects on consumer prices) would, it said, raise about $US900 billion over a decade and those on Canada and Brazil more than $US50 billion between them – so about $US950 billion in total. That’s only about 56 per cent of the revenue forgone as a result of the Supreme Court’s ruling and, in the context of total US government revenues of more than $US5.6 trillion a year (or the “Department of Wars’ $US1.5 trillion budget request) almost immaterial. Tariff revenues, if they don’t evaporate as a result of the continuing legal actions, aren’t going to solve America’s debt and deficit problems; indeed, they are more likely to exacerbate them because they raise the inflation rate and subtract from economic activity. Whatever Trump and his officials might believe, or at least say, his tariffs are a tax on US businesses and households. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York has calculated that about 90 per cent of their cost is absorbed by domestic businesses and consumers. Loading

Advertisement

The tariffs cost jobs, add up to 70 basis points to the inflation rate and subtract about 0.2 percentage points from US GDP, along with the damage they do to the global economy. There is a view that, whatever tariff revenue the Supreme Court leaves intact will last beyond the point where Trump departs the White House, with Congress, regardless of the party in control, unlikely to voluntarily abandon a revenue stream, albeit one that is a regressive tax on consumers. That’s because America’s finances are parlous, and deteriorating. Trump added $US7.8 trillion to the national debt in his first term, and Joe Biden another $US8 trillion, though both those presidencies were coloured by massive pandemic-driven spending. So far in this term – without a pandemic – Trump has added another $US3.2 trillion, raising gross federal government debt to $US39.3 trillion, or about 125 per cent of US GDP.

Advertisement

The interest bill on that debt is more than $US1 trillion and is rising sharply, influenced significantly by Trump’s policies. Whatever Trump and his officials might believe, or at least say, his tariffs are a tax on US businesses and households. The tariffs, and the war in the Middle East particularly, have pushed up the US inflation rate and have had a marked impact on bond yields. On February 27, the day before the US and Israel attacked Iran, the US 10-year bond yield was 3.94 per cent. Today it is 4.68 per cent. The two-year yield was 3.38 per cent. Now it is 4.33 per cent. With the US Treasury, over several administrations, increasingly raising debt of shorter duration because it was the cheapest segment of the yield curve, about a third of all existing US government debt on issue has to be refinanced this year.

Those higher yields on its bonds mean a government interest bill that already tops a trillion dollars can only increase – relatively minor movement in bond yields can add tens of billions, if not hundreds of billions, to the annual interest bill. Related Article Updated

It would have added up to five professions of love for a new culture, a new code and making history, in 17 months. Even in a time when a signature on a contract is barely worth the price of the ink, a Lomax commitment is clearly a fungible token. For the Chiefs, who have become too big to fail, signing Lomax is a smart play – he’s high-profile, he’s an Origin player, and he’s still only 26 – and another sign of the club’s lust for immediate, up-front success while building its long-term Marshall Plan for Pacific domination. Zac Lomax, in action for the Western Force, will move back to league in 2028 with the PNG Chiefs. Getty Images As for Lomax’s motives, he dropped the biggest clue when, after moving to rugby union a few months ago, he said: “I don’t want to get to the end of my career and think about, you know, should I have given that a crack.” He’s certainly not going to regret any roads not taken.

Doueihi or don’t he? In a curious juxtaposition of events leading into the weekend, there was speculation about Latrell Mitchell and Tom Trbojevic having their pay reduced because of how many matches they miss with injury, while the Tigers’ Adam Doueihi, who has received many months’ worth of paid injury time in his career, chose not to play at all if selected at lock. The Tigers have stood by Adam Doueihi as he has recovered from many injuries. Getty Images The contrast was glaring. You had two superstars whose disappointment must be even greater than their fans’, injured when trying too hard to get on the field, then being implicitly criticised for not justifying their pay packets.

Advertisement

And on the other hand, you had a first-grader deciding against playing because (his version reportedly) he wanted to highlight “issues” within the club. Wayne Bennett said, rightly, that docking injured players’ pay was a ridiculous idea. It is at complete odds with rugby league’s DNA as a sport aligned with the rise of the labour movement. In a fair system, a worker is not penalised for bad luck. A crestfallen Tom Trbojevic comes off injured against the Gold Coast. Fox Sports But docking the pay of a worker who decides not to turn up? Hmm. In his press conference after the Tigers’ loss to Canberra, coach Benji Marshall walked on eggshells. He said of his players: “This is their job they get paid pretty well to do, so you’ve got to go out there and do your job.”

Advertisement

Then, when questioned about whether a voluntary non-player (Doueihi) deserved his pay, Marshall said: “We’re also in a world where if you don’t feel mentally right to play, you can’t make him play. It’s tough, we’re men, we have feelings, we’re in a day and age where you need to express those feelings, and he did.” Let’s just say Doueihi was allowed a week of paid compassionate leave. Fainu comeback too much even for rugby league “Jailed ex-Manly hooker wanted to play league wearing an ankle bracelet” is not only the best rugby league headline of 2026 but the most rugby league headline of 2026. Manase Fainu was, in 2019, a very promising NRL hooker for Manly and a linchpin of the club’s plans to build a premiership-winning team around the Fainu and Trbojevic families.

It all came unstuck when Manase attacked someone at a Mormon church dance with a knife he pulled out of the sling he was wearing for an injured shoulder (the story kept getting more and more rugby league). Then Manly Sea Eagles hooker Manase Fainu outside court in 2022. Rhett Wyman Now on weekend release after serving his custodial sentence, Fainu has recently applied to play A grade for the Alexandria Rovers. The NSWRL knocked him back on several grounds, including the risk of him causing an injury with his ankle bracelet. A donk on the head from a heavy-duty, impact-resistant polycarbonate GPS device would be a novel excuse for missing a tackle. You’d have thought Corrective Services could easily trace Fainu without the bracelet while he was on the field, but we don’t make the rules.

Russell Packer set a precedent for returning to the NRL in 2016 after serving a prison term for assault, and ARL Commission chairman Peter V’landys is known to like redemption stories on the scale of Greek mythology. But in today’s NRL, a Manase Fainu comeback would require more twists and unlikely favours from the gods than Odysseus’ comeback from Troy. Christmas in July Cronulla are playing better than anyone in the NRL, which makes them the premiers if the grand final was in July. Related Article Manly 12 Cronulla 48

The Sharks would be the envy of Newcastle, who have just lost the Dylans, Brown and Lucas, for the season and Kalyn Ponga for weeks. Melbourne are without Cameron Munster and Harry Grant among others, North Queensland Tom Dearden, the Dolphins Isaiya Katoa and Souths and Manly have the NRL’s longest casualty lists. title: The green light is on for tax returns. One thing won't get your refund faster

IN BRIEF The ATO has loaded a vast amount of data into its systems to make lodging tax returns easier and more accurate.

The ATO uses data matching to detect incorrect claims and may delay refunds while suspicious returns are checked.

The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) says taxpayers with straightforward tax affairs can now begin lodging their tax returns, with most income statements and pre-fill information now available.

More than 100 million pieces of data from employers, banks, private health insurers, share registries and government agencies have been loaded into the ATO's systems to help people lodge more accurately and with less effort.

ATO assistant commissioner Anita Challen released a statement saying that most income statements and pre-fill information is now available.

"If you're self-lodging, before you hit submit, take a few extra minutes to check your details to avoid delays and mistakes," she said.

The ATO is also expanding its pre-fill services this year to include income reported through the Taxable Payment Annual Report.

From late August, contractors in some industries — including construction, cleaning, courier services, information technology, road freight and security — may see that income automatically added to their returns.

Do I have 'straightforward' tax affairs?

Your tax affairs are likely to be straightforward if you're primarily paying tax on salary and wages, with only a small amount of taxable investment income or government payments.

If you're applying for more than basic deductions, or your return includes elements like capital gains, receipt of rental payments and foreign income, your return may not be straightforward.

If you're unsure, you should consult a tax accountant or services such as the ATO's Tax Help or National Tax Clinic for advice.

Common mistakes taxpayers should avoid

The ATO is also warning Australians against overclaiming deductions or failing to declare all sources of income.

That includes earnings from side hustles, cash jobs, rental properties and online content creation.

The agency says it uses sophisticated data-matching systems to detect suspicious claims and may delay refunds while returns are investigated.

Taxpayers are also being urged not to simply copy deductions from previous years if their work or circumstances have changed.

The ATO is reminding Australians that the proposed $1,000 standard work-related deduction does not apply this tax time and cannot be claimed until the 2027 tax year.

It is also warning people not to rely on tax advice from artificial intelligence platforms, social media "finfluencers", family or friends without checking official guidance or speaking to a registered tax professional.

Before lodging, the ATO recommends taxpayers check their personal details, bank account and superannuation information are up to date and ensure all pre-filled information is accurate.

It also encourages people to keep records of deductions, use the ATO app to track their return and remain alert to scams.

The tax office says it will never send unsolicited messages containing links asking people to log in or provide personal information.

Most tax returns are processed within 12 business days, according to the ATO, which says calling the agency will not speed up the process.

People lodging their own tax return have until 31 October, while those using a registered tax agent may have longer, provided they are on their agent's books before that date.

title: Australia's favourite holiday destination is undergoing a hidden transformation
text:
Since Bali's main landfill site, Suwung, closed in April, bags of rubbish and single-use plastics have piled up in the streets, on the beaches and in the canals.

The rest is burned.

"The air is no longer fresh; the views are clouded by haze; and the sweet scent of frangipani has been replaced by the acrid smell of burning plastic," Balinese writer Sugi Lanus posted on social media.

In June the Balinese government partially reopened the landfill to organic waste, limited to two days a week. Officials had wanted to close it for years, as the central Indonesian government pushes to end open-air waste dumping.

At the same time, tourism to Bali has hit an all-time peak. Last year, visitors increased by nearly 10 per cent to hit just under seven million visitors.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Australians made up 1.6 million of those, according to the government's statistics bureau.

But as Indonesia paves the way for more tourists, with a master plan to transform Bali into the "Dubai" of Southeast Asia, it's the local communities who are left to shoulder the burden of Bali's environmental emergency.

Waste is a 'political issue'

Made Suarnatha, who started environmental NGO Wisnu Foundation in Bali in 1993, told SBS News Bali's waste crisis was "a political issue".

He said the landfill closure masked an existing problem with the transition from mostly organic waste to plastic waste — a problem intensified by tourism.

"You come here as a tourist, you need food, you need water, you make trips here and there, so you bring waste as a consequence," he said.

The closure of Bali's main landfill site in April made the island's waste crisis more visible. Source: Supplied / Gde Sugiarta/Wisnu Foundation

"It's no big issue when we talk about waste which is mostly organic, but the tourism industry comes, and the character of the waste changes to packaging with plastic, cardboard, metal, and everything," he said.

"It changed its character without being followed by an understanding of how to handle it."

Putu Natih, an economist at Universitas Indonesia, grew up visiting family in Bali.

She told SBS News that of the roughly 3,436 tonnes of waste generated every day in Bali, around 40 per cent is burned or illegally dumped.

"The failure is more likely structural rather than behavioural. The regulation exists, but the collection and processing infrastructure to back it up does not," Natih said.

On 12 July, environmental group Wahli Bali and student activists Frontier Bali staged a protest in the Bali capital Denpasar calling for a moratorium on tourism until the waste crisis had been addressed, also campaigning against what they see as water and land-use crises.

Source: SBS News

However, with visitors to Bali making up 45 per cent of Indonesia's overall tourism in 2025, the government is instead looking for ways to boost foreign investment in the island.

The new Dubai?

In April, the Indonesian government opened a new Kawasan Ekonomi Khusus or 'KEK', on a 498-hectare island joined to Bali by a causeway. It's called Kura Kura, or Turtle Island.

The KEK is a special economic zone offering 20-year tax holidays to foreign investors, luring them with luxury residential and shopping developments similar to the Dubai International Financial Centre.

"We will make it in a way that our financial centre is on Dubai's calibre," Indonesia's coordinating minister for economic affairs Airlangga Hartarto told reporters in June, as quoted in the Jakarta Globe.

Several facilities have already opened on the island, including a high-end shopping centre with a rooftop pool.

Natih said if the KEK had strong safeguards, like anti-money laundering oversight and rules against profit-shifting, it could be an opportunity for genuine economic development.

"I would be careful about calling it a tax haven," Natih said.

"Ultimately, the goal should be to attract businesses that can create real value, employment and innovation in Bali, not simply capital seeking lower taxes."

According to Natih, foreign investment in Bali in 2025 already sat at around 25.6 trillion rupees, or $379.39 billion.

"Foreign investment has become a major driver of Bali's economy," she said.

"The important question is not how much investment Bali receives, but what kind?" Natih said.

"Unless investors contribute to infrastructure needs to support growth, local communities end up carrying many of the environmental and social costs," Natih said.

Natih on a recent research trip to North Bali to speak to locals about waste. Source: Supplied

"Development should strengthen the relationship between people, culture and nature, not weaken it."

'Jakarta policy'

Bali has the lowest rate of unemployment in Indonesia, according to the government's Badan Pusat Statistik.

In August 2025, the unemployment rate sat at 1.49 per cent, compared to the national average of 4.85 per cent.

While foreign investment brings more jobs, the local Balinese are in "tight competition" with job seekers from other islands or foreigners.

READ MORE The awkward new rules about to kick in for travellers to Bali

Suarnatha said the spoils of the tourism industry aren't evenly distributed across the island.

"Not all foreigners coming to Bali is a tourist now, they are also seeking for jobs, and they'll create their own jobs here in Bali."

Suarnatha criticised what he called "Jakarta policy", centralised decision-making about Bali in which the community had little say.

"We rely on Jakarta...whatever decisions from Jakarta structurally, the regulation influence a lot of issues."

"It's confusing, there's no power to say 'no', and then investment goes up."

However, Suarnatha said there are positive ways for tourists to contribute to the island's sustainability.

"Actually tourists can put pressure...the Australian government can share the pressure onto the Bali government or Indonesian government," Suarnatha said.

He also called on visitors to be aware, and to spread awareness of the challenges Bali faces.

"I love my island, but my island its also feeling sad."

title: 2026 Census: Who must complete it and is it compulsory?
text:
IN BRIEF The 2026 Census is compulsory for everyone in Australia on Tuesday 11 August.

The questionnaire is in English but translators and interpreters are available for non-English speakers.

The Census is run by the Australian government every five years — but Peter Doukas, chair of the Federation of Ethnic Communities' Councils of Australia (FECCA), believes it's important to remember this questionnaire is strictly "apolitical".

Since 1911, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) has conducted the Census of Population and Housing, regardless of the political party in power. Data collected is used to inform decisions around the funding and location of schools, transport and health care services.

Doukas told SBS News the Census also provides valuable information on the demographic makeup of multicultural communities.

"It's not [about] taking a political side ... it's also not allowing the cynicism of government to get in the way of the important role that the ABS holds in collecting ... accurate demographic data about what makes up Australia," he said.

This year, the Census will be held on Tuesday 11 August. The last Census was on 10 August 2021.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Is the Census compulsory?

The Census must be completed by every person in Australia on Census night. That includes visitors to the country, regardless of how long they have been in Australia or how long they plan to stay.

Generally, one person per household fills out the form.

People will soon receive a letter directing them to complete the Census online. Paper forms can also be requested if preferred. Credit: ABS

International visitors staying in hotels, motels, or other holiday accommodation can access paper Census forms. People staying in short-term rental accommodation (like an Airbnb or Stayz) can complete the Census online with internet access.

Do temporary visa holders need to complete the Census?

Migrants, refugees and people on temporary visas (including international students and tourists) must also complete the Census.

Doukas said people are "not giving away private information" that could be "used against them" by participating in the survey.

Confidential information, such as names and addresses, cannot be accessed by police or immigration agents.

The Census aims to capture everyone in Australia at a particular point in time, like a family photograph of the nation. Source: AAP / Jane Dempster

Online information about the Census is also available in 26 different languages via the ABS website. However, the questionnaire must be completed in English.

People who speak a language other than English can contact the Translating and Interpreting Service (TIS National) which provides access to interpreters who speak more than 150 languages.

People staying in remote and regional Australia, including fly-in fly-out workers, are expected to complete the Census.

Around 30,000 ABS field staff have been employed to ensure all Australians, including people experiencing homelessness or in hospital, can access the form. Field staff will also gather Census information from people in police custody on 11 August.

The ABS confirmed to SBS News that they receive administrative data for people in detention centres and correctional facilities within Australia which provides necessary Census details.

What happens if you provide false information?

The Census asks up to 66 questions, including an individual's gender identity, ancestry and religious affiliation.

When asked about religion during the first-ever Census in 1911, 32 people identified as "Wowser" and 21 as "Angelic". In the 2011 Census, more than 64,000 people in Australia marked their religion as "Jedi".

The ABS maintains "every response matters" during the Census and helps determine the distribution of public funds. Providing false or misleading statements or information is considered an offence and can result in a fine of up to $3,640.

title: Albanese flags new fuel announcements as petrol prices tipped to spike further
text:
In Brief The Prime Minister said his government was not planning to extend the fuel excise discount past 31 July.

He has indicated there is funding for additional measures but has not said what they are.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says his government is not planning to extend the fuel excise discount but has foreshadowed there will be further announcements on fuel in the coming days.

The 32 cents a litre fuel excise discount expired 30 June but was extended by another month at 16 cents a litre.

That discount is set to expire 2 August, at which point Australian drivers will no longer be shielded from price increases at the bowser.

Petrol and diesel prices have risen sharply in the past week. In Melbourne, unleaded rose six per cent to $1.80 per litre, while diesel rose 12 per cent to $2.17.

In Sydney, the average regular unleaded petrol price rose 10 cents per litre to 171.5 cents per litre and diesel fuel rose 22.0 cents per litre to 209.2 cents per litre, according to the NRMA.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Regionally, the NRMA said the average price of unleaded rose 5.7 cents per litre, while diesel went by 17.4 cents per litre.

The NRMA said it expected prices to rise further when the fuel excise discount comes to an end next Sunday, amidst rising wholesale costs.

Global oil prices soared this week, with Brent crude spiking above US$100 a barrel for the first time since May.

Albanese was asked on the ABC's Insiders program whether his government was considering a further extension of the excise discount.

"That's not in our planning at this point in time," the prime minister said, adding that the government would deal with cost of living issues "as they arise".

He said his government had set aside $10 billion dollars for a fuel security plan and hinted that more of this funding was going to be allocated.

"That [the fuel security plan] was about better fuel security going forward, including a government-owned reserve," he said.

"We'll have some more announcements about fuel in the coming days and weeks as well."

He would not say whether these "announcements" related to fuel supply or storage, saying Australians would have to wait for the details.

The statement comes as the ongoing war in the Middle East and the Houthi Rebel blockade of the Bab al-Mandab Strait continues to create chaos in global energy markets by restricting oil trade.

Around seven per cent of the world's oil output now transits through Bab al-Mandab, off the coast of Yemen. Experts say a blockade there could push prices into the US$120–150 per barrel range— creating further concern for domestic energy supplies.

Albanese said that figures released on Sunday showed fuel usage had "come down" since the US's strikes against Iran sparked a war in the Middle East and led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz early this year.

"It's lower than it was a year ago."

"That’s a good thing ... the longer [the war] goes, the bigger the conflict, the bigger the impact will be.

"This is a war on the other side of the world; we are not protagonists in it, but we are impacted by it, and we’ve consistently called for a de-escalation, and we’ll continue to do so."

According to federal government data, the country has 42 days of petrol, 38 days of diesel and 32 days of jet fuel — all higher stocks than the country had in the March 2026 quarter.

Will raise tariff concerns

Albanese also hit out at the Trump administration's announcement of a new round of trade tariffs on Friday, after it accused Australia of not doing enough on modern slavery.

Many Australian exports to the US will now be subject to a 12.5 per cent tariff, replacing a temporary 10 per cent levy that the Trump administration introduced earlier this year.

The prime minister said he would "absolutely" be raising the "unjustified" tariff with his American counterpart.

"We’ll raise it at every level of the Australia-US relationship," he said.

"This will lead to higher costs in the United States and undermine the trading relationship that we have with our US friends."

title: Why your hairdresser might not know how to cut your curls
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Veronica Vazquez has always had curly hair, but she hasn't always embraced it.

Growing up in the countryside, she says her curls made her stand out.

"Everyone had straight blonde hair. I remember going to school, getting water from the bubbler and flattening all my hair down because it was just too much," she tells SBS News.

Inheriting her curls from her Spanish father, Vazquez says her mother, who is of Malaysian heritage, didn't have the tools or knowledge to style and manage curly hair.

Now a mother herself, she has watched her nine-year-old daughter, Ivory, who also has curly hair, face the same challenges of standing out among her peers at school.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

She says she's determined to break the cycle and empower her daughter to feel confident about her appearance.

Veronica Vazquez is determined to give her daughter the confidence to embrace her curly hair, something she says took her years to learn herself. Source: SBS News

"I just have to embrace, educate and show her all the beautiful styles that are possible with curly hair."

For many Australians with curly, coily and afro-textured hair, finding a hairdresser with the right skills remains a challenge. Stylists say the problem starts in the classroom, where training has long failed to keep pace with the needs of textured hair.

Finding a stylist who understands curls

A horror haircut is a common experience within the curly hair community.

Unlike straight hair, curly, coily, afro or textured hair has a different structure that requires specialised cutting techniques. Experienced stylists often cut textured hair while it is dry to better understand how the curls fall and frame the face.

Vazquez and her daughter travel nearly two hours to Curl Lab in Sydney, a salon specialising in curly hair cuts and education, but she says it took years of trial and error to find the right place.

"We went to one salon, and they straightened Ivory's hair and cut it. Unfortunately, her hair is never straight, so by the time we've gone home, showered, the curls bounced up and it was just chopped everywhere," she says.

It's really no fault of the stylist; they're just not educated in how to cut curly hair.

Curl Lab owner Natasha Thandekafountas says the current hair education system teaches students the same cutting techniques for clients with both straight and textured or afro hair, rather than providing training tailored to different hair types.

"If you're cutting curly hair when it's straightened or wet, it's going to look good until the curls bounce up," Thandekafountas tells SBS News.

Sydney-based salon owner Natasha Thandekafountas says the current hair education system fails to tailor cutting techniques to different hair types. Source: SBS News

"We like to call it the 'Lord Farquaad' bob, so many clients come in for us to fix that," referring to the character from the film Shrek, who has a pageboy bob haircut.

How history shaped hair standards

The challenges faced by many people with curly and afro-textured hair are rooted in decades of beauty standards that experts say favoured straight hair.

Early anthropologists and naturalists once used the colour and texture of hair as markers of social hierarchy.

Farida Fozdar, a sociologist and professor of anthropology at Curtin University, says hair texture, much like race, was historically used to reinforce ideas about status, with so-called 'Caucasian hair' — blonde, light coloured or straight hair — often viewed as the ideal.

"There was a bit of a tendency to assume kinky, or curly hair was somehow abnormal or a lesser quality of hair," she tells SBS News.

"There were a number of researchers who described it as 'woolly' hair, suggesting it was more like animals."

Fozdar says those attitudes began to shift as Australia became more culturally diverse following the end of the White Australia policy and the increase in migration from the 1960s onwards.

"People who migrated in the 60s, 70s and 80s found it very difficult to find hair salons, but there is a growing awareness about the need to cater to populations who are different," she says.

While specialist salons are now becoming more common, many stylists say education and training have struggled to keep pace with Australia's diverse population.

Why hairdressing education is falling short

More than a decade ago, afro and curly hair education became part of the national training curriculum developed by Service and Creative Skills Australia (SaCSA), the Jobs and Skills Council for personal services.

However, the content is delivered as optional training in some qualifications, meaning many apprentice hairdressers can complete their studies with little or no practical experience working with textured hair.

In some states, including NSW, there's an elective unit on using a protein treatment to relax curly hair that teaches professionals to analyse hair, select products, apply heat, and smooth curls.

Amelia Canet, a curl stylist based in Sydney, says the standard hairdressing training qualification doesn't adequately cover the basics.

Many hair stylists say hairdressing and barbering training has struggled to keep pace with Australia's diverse population. Source: SBS News

"There wasn't any curl education at all. If we did have any textured clients, we were told just blow-dry them," she tells SBS News.

Other curly stylists, like Tulsi Prasad, say they had to take matters into their own hands and teach themselves to cut and style textured hair.

"I just had to learn on my own, watch my own videos, do my own private course, but go through TAFE to learn the proper ways to do everything else," she tells SBS News.

Salon owner Thandekafountas says she invests heavily in training because graduates often arrive without the skills needed to confidently work with textured hair. She sets aside a portion of the business budget to train new staff.

"We need to catch up. Close that gap and really have things mainstreamed," she says.

"How come we're not being serviced in the same way someone with straight hair is?"

It's not just hair; it's our identity, it's our culture, and for so long we've been told that it's too big, it's too busy, it's not professional. So we really want to change that image.

The push for curriculum reform

In March 2025, SaCSA began reviewing and updating its standards for some of the hairdressing and barbering qualifications to ensure they align with current industry practice and workforce needs.

Part of its proposal includes recommendations for three new units focusing on cutting and colouring curly and coily hair.

Natalie Turmine, CEO of SaCSA, says learners will also gain knowledge of the history and culture of curly and coily hair, but adds there isn't enough demand in the industry for the units to become compulsory parts of the curriculum.

"As demand and industry become more aware and more customers are coming in and that demand builds, then we'll be able to look at potentially building in skill sets and building it in as a mandatory part of the qualification," she tells SBS News.

SaCSA is undertaking a review of some hairdressing and barbering qualifications to ensure they align with current industry practice and workforce needs. Source: SBS News

For the hairdressing industry, the recommendations represent more than just new training units — they signal growing recognition of the need for textured hair education.

Fiona Beamish, CEO of the Australian Hairdressing Council, says the proposed reforms are a significant first step and hopes the units will eventually become compulsory.

"Data tells us that we are ready for this training package to include these units and I'd like to think in the future we could have this as a mandatory training package," she tells SBS News.

Driving change from within the industry

The push for better training comes as the hairdressing industry continues to grapple with a shortage of skilled workers.

According to Jobs and Skills Australia, only 45 per cent of advertised hairdressing roles were filled in 2022-23, with 85 per cent of applicants deemed unsuitable.

A 2026 SaCSA report examining the drivers behind the hairdressing workforce shortage found the sustainability issue is largely linked to "outdated course content and insufficient workforce preparation", raising broader questions about whether current training is meeting the industry's needs.

READ MORE How a hairdressing client list became a campaign to help Jay and Jeremy become dads

Sydney hairstylist and educator Chrissy Zemura has spent years delivering private courses and professional education, and creating products for customers with textured hair.

In 2020, she started an online petition calling for a mandatory module on curly and afro-textured hair, which attracted more than 42,000 signatures.

"While the curriculum is the mountain peak, a lot has changed over the past six years, including people's mindsets," Zemura tells SBS News.

SaCSA says the updated training recommendations are in the final stages of review with state and federal departments. They will then be assessed by the Assurance Body before the new training package is published early next year.

title: 'Very volatile stock': A caution to Tesla investors as Musk doubles down on AI
text:
in brief Tesla's profits have dropped after heavy investment in artificial intelligence weighed on earnings.

Some experts say companies may have to invest heavily in AI to stay competitive in the future.

Financial analysts have warned not to expect much stability in Tesla's share price after CEO Elon Musk defended billions of dollars of investment at the electric vehicle manufacturer, which has just seen one of its worst stock market falls in years.

This week, Tesla reported second-quarter profit of $US1.1 billion ($1.57 billion), down about 5 per cent from a year earlier, as lower vehicle prices and heavy investment in artificial intelligence weighed on the company's earnings.

The result translated to 33 cents a share, well below analysts' expectations of 53 cents, while revenue rose 26 per cent to $28.2 billion.

Although Tesla beat expectations for second-quarter vehicle deliveries earlier this month, the company said profitability was hit by lower vehicle selling prices, reduced revenue from regulatory credits and unspecified "energy warranty-related charges".

Capital expenditure more than doubled to $5.8 billion ($8.3 billion) during the quarter as Tesla accelerated investment in AI and manufacturing.

Tesla is embarking on a massive construction spree that Musk characterised on a conference call as probably the United States' "fastest industrial scale-up since World War Two".

The company said production of its Cybercab had begun in Texas, the Tesla Semi remained on track for 2026, and subscriptions to its Full Self-Driving driver-assistance program continued to grow.

Asked about scaling Tesla's robotaxi business, Musk said the company was focused on achieving near-perfect reliability.

"How many nines of reliability do you need to scale?" Musk said. "Ideally, you want 99.99999, you know, per cent reliable."

AI investments are 'very expensive'

Tesla's spending has drawn scrutiny from investors concerned about returns on its AI investments.

CFRA Research analyst Garrett Nelson said uncertainty over the spending had weighed on Tesla shares.

"They just haven't been very transparent with [Wall] Street on the expected return of the dollars that have been spent."

Jai Mirchandani, chief executive of Elm Responsible Investments, said the spending reflected Tesla's long-term strategy.

"The company and Musk is saying that it's one of the best investment opportunities and that's why they're investing so heavily in AI and robotics primarily," he told SBS News.

"As we've seen from companies like even Google and Microsoft and all the tech leaders, it's very expensive, and it requires a lot of capital to build the AI infrastructure and technology.

"And if you want to succeed in this space, our view is that you have to be investing in AI and innovation."

Mirchandani described AI as a revolutionary technology that needs "a lot of capital investment".

Musk defends Tesla spending

Musk said Tesla's capital expenditure (capex) was justified, saying the company "should be spending on capex as fast as we can spend ... without it being too wasteful".

"It's OK to be a little less capital efficient if we get things done sooner."

Tesla's chief financial officer Vaibhav Taneja said research and development costs would "continue to grow in 2026 and beyond".

Speculation has also grown about closer ties between Tesla and SpaceX following the rocket company's stock market debut, although Musk declined to discuss any potential combination.

READ MORE Musk becomes first trillionaire in history as SpaceX shares soar

"There's more and more overlap," said Musk.

"Obviously, we can't talk about combining companies and that kind of thing on an earnings call. It's got to be done with the appropriate process."

Mirchandani cautioned investors about Tesla's share price movements.

"The reality is that Tesla is a very volatile stock. And so I'd sort of just be mindful of that."

Watch and see

Stockbroker Richard Hemming said investors were increasingly rewarding companies that continued to innovate.

"I think the innovation part of it is more worrying for investors for companies that don't innovate," he told SBS News.

"I think that, in the next reporting season, it's going to be interesting to see how companies ... are going in the sales line. "

He said Australia's upcoming corporate reporting season would provide an important test of company profitability.

"We are seeing sort of signs, especially in Australia, that productivity's falling," he said.

"Productivity in Australia has been under a lot of pressure versus the rest of the world because I guess we're not seeing the kind of innovation that they're seeing in the US.

"So definitely, the upcoming results are going to be very, very important. "

title: The momentary slip that only showed Albanese's escalating control of the Labor Party
text:
IN BRIEF The 50th national conference of the Australian Labor Party was held in Adelaide over the last few days.

The conference was almost entirely devoid of the passionate and public policy brawls once seen at such events.

"We are proudly a progressive movement: two words that can't be applied to the escalator in this building," Anthony Albanese said to much mirth at Friday's Labor Party conference dinner.

The viral moment — in which the prime minister's descent came to a sudden, jolting stop, followed by an expletive-laden reaction — was one of the very few times this week that the veteran Labor party animal didn't appear to have a level of mastery over events that unfolded in Adelaide at Labor's once-a-term policy palooza.

With his gag lapped up by the crowd of party faithful, many of whom paid a door charge of $135 to attend the gala dinner, Albanese continued:

"When it [the escalator] did come to a standstill, I'll admit there was a moment, just a moment, when the ladder of opportunity finally made sense," he said, riffing on former leader Mark Latham's ill-fated slogan from 2004, one of the party's more recent political low-points.

Two decades on, having achieved Labor's most powerful parliamentary majority in history, the prime minister said the party "can finally laugh about making him leader".

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

While the glow may have dimmed in the wider electorate, judging by recent polling, Albanese seemingly retained the halo of that 2025 election result among the delegates who 'debated' the party's platform this week.

The conference's myriad factions moved deftly to almost entirely avoid the passionate and public policy brawls of the past, which Albanese, the apex predator of the Labor left, used to once involve himself in.

VAD motion sees rare moment of debate

All but one of the various amendments and motions was passed with unanimous support on the floor.

The sole outlier, a commitment for the government to remove barriers around using telehealth to access voluntary assisted dying (VAD), allowed a sole delegate to speak against the motion, the sole amendment to pass where some delegates voted against.

The party also enshrined in its constitution a conscience vote for MPs on this issue, similar to that allowed on abortion.

Trade Minister Don Farrell — a longtime Labor right power-broker who remains opposed to euthanasia — rejected suggestions debate was being suppressed among delegates.

"Far from a graveyard, this is a flowering of democracy," Farrell told the floor on Saturday to much applause.

Husic's Gaza resolution dropped

Backbench MP Ed Husic had a far more pessimistic assessment, arguing that a perception has formed among Labor MPs that "taking a different stand or taking different ground presents a risk to the stability of government".

The former industry minister has found liberation in his backbench demotion by fashioning himself as a rebel with no shortage of causes.

Beyond his well-known divergences with party colleagues on Israel and Gaza, he's also pushed for a new gas tax and a rethink of AUKUS.

On Friday, he called for the government to implement the outstanding elements of the Uluru Statement from the Heart.

But despite claiming some credit for the government's decision to recognise Palestinian statehood last year, his advocacy this year ultimately led to nought in Adelaide.

He cut a lone, isolated figure on Saturday morning roaming the cavernous halls of the Adelaide Convention Centre, as he learned he'd lost the support he required to put up a rival resolution on the Gaza war.

"You've got to be able to find a way to disagree respectfully and try and work with people and have that discussion," Husic told journalists shortly after it became clear his support had evaporated.

READ MORE UN accuses Hamas of hampering aid as EU pledges billions to rebuild Gaza

Husic's resolution, as seen by this correspondent, was ambitious in its language.

It called on Labor's platform to acknowledge a 2024 International Court of Justice ruling that Israel's legal actions in the West Bank breach International conventions on apartheid, and that the party expressed alarm over the UN independent commission of inquiry's findings of Israeli-conducted genocide against Palestinians — both of which Israel refutes.

The resolution also advocated a ramp-up in sanctions on Israel, the prosecution of dual nationals alleged to have committed war crimes with the Israeli military, and for the government to withdraw defence co-operation and diplomatic personnel from the Australian embassy in Tel Aviv.

The chance of it being allowed to go to a debate seems even more remote, given the criticism expressed by other groups, including the Israeli embassy, that the draft platform had been too soft on Hamas, having omitted a call for the group to disarm from the wording.

In the conference's fringe area, where the panels among punters presented far more of an ideological contest than the conference floor, a booth set aside for Labor Friends of Israel was left empty on the event's opening day, and removed by the weekend.

"To be able to have those discussions is a sign of strength, not a sign of weakness," the Western Sydney MP said, mimicking one of the prime minister's favourite bits of Medicare stage play by flaunting his own Labor membership card.

"They can put me in the freezer, I don't give a sh-t."

Jewish-Palestinian duo support current position

Husic's hastily called press conference clashed with the start of the foreign policy debate, meaning he walked onto the floor midway through back-to-back speeches from Jewish MP Josh Burns and Palestinian Australian MP Basem Abdo in support of the unamended foreign policy platform.

Burns said both he and Abdo were "fathers who dream of taking their children to a land free from conflict" and spoke positively of the solidarity shared by his colleague in the aftermath of the Bondi terror attack, as well as the importance of recognising the pain of others.

Abdo, who since being elected in 2025 has kept a low profile in parliament on the war, spoke about the occupation experienced by generations of Palestinians, conceding "no single motion can do justice" to the challenges experienced in recent years by both of their communities.

READ MORE Israeli troops shoot dead seven-month-old Palestinian baby in the occupied West Bank

The Albanese-era Labor Party has ultimately been successful in making this conference a showcase of unity in purpose, with any show of dissent successfully cauterised by the countless closed-door discussions between Labor's myriad factions, away from the cameras of the substantial media pack.

It makes the passionate on-stage embrace between Burns and Abdo, which merited a lengthy standing ovation, stand out even more.

title: 2026 Census Australia: Key dates, what's included and why it matters
text:
Every five years, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) counts every person and every household in the country as part of the Census of Population and Housing.

That includes Australians, young and old, from metropolitan and rural Australia. Even holidaymakers, international students and temporary visa holders are counted on Census night. It's often referred to as the most comprehensive snapshot of Australia, akin to a family photograph of the country.

This year, the Census will take place on Tuesday 11 August.

Emily Walter, Census national spokesperson at the ABS, said it's about more than just numbers. She believes the Census tells a story of a changing Australia.

"Our Census provides a snapshot of the country at a point in time ... So, it's really important that absolutely everyone is reflected in the Census," she told SBS Urdu.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"It is compulsory for that very good reason, and it's important that we get a very accurate count of the number of people in Australia ... because it's about providing data for the country to help serve the country."

What the Census measures

The first population count in Australia dates back to 1788. In 1911, the ABS ran its first national Census, with field officers travelling by horse or bicycle to collect information about Australians.

Generally, one person completes the Census form for the entire household. The Census can be completed online or on paper. Credit: Australian Bureau of Statistics

Today, the Census is available online and by paper and can also be completed with help from Census field staff.

It's compulsory for everyone in Australia to complete the Census. Generally, one person from each household completes the Census — although you can ask for separate forms for privacy reasons.

If an Australian is overseas on Census night, they don't need to complete the Census.

The ABS collects personal information about individuals, including age, country of birth, cultural background, living situation, work and education. Some questions about religious affiliation, gender and sexual orientation (for people aged 16 and over) will be optional.

All information collected is confidential and protected by law.

What is Census data used for?

Census data is used to inform decisions about language services, settlement support, transport, schools, health care, infrastructure and business. It also helps plan local services for individuals, families and communities.

SBS broadcasts and publishes across more than 60 languages, using data from the Census to ensure its audio, digital, and television offerings reflect the country's evolving demographics.

The data is often used by researchers to study a range of topics, including population demographics, economic trends and social issues.

The 2021 Census counted over 25 million people in Australia, excluding overseas visitors. That was an 8.6 per cent increase compared to 2016. Source: AAP

Liz Allen, a demographer at the Australian National University's Centre for Social Policy Research, said the Census provides an "important suite of information" for decision-makers.

"We've seen internationally what happens when the statistical undertaking of a Census is compromised. That means that we lose vital information, data is unable to be published ... that then leads to policymakers making decisions basically blindfolded, and it especially harms people in minority groups," she said.

She also believes the Census provides the nation with an opportunity to pause and plan for Australia's future.

"The Census for me is not just about data.

"It's about us coming together as a nation, being seen, being captured in that family photograph and ensuring that the future of this country will be data-informed and policy will reflect exactly who we are."

title: 'Life delayed': The $11,710 bill keeping some couples apart
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Bringing a partner to Australia has long been a costly and time-consuming process.

As of this month, applicants now face a record application fee of $11,710 — up $2,345 from the previous charge — while many continue to wait well over a year for a decision, leaving couples separated for months and, in some cases, years.

For Sarosh Akram, the increase came just as he was preparing to apply for his wife's offshore partner visa.

"It's made me think harder about how to save enough to lodge the application sooner, so I can start my wait in the Department [of Home Affairs'] queue," the 32-year-old tells SBS News.

Living in Parkes, a town in the central west of NSW, Akram is now exploring ways to cut costs and grow his savings to cover the additional amount required to apply.

This has further complicated my situation and delayed my life, which I intended to start with my partner in Australia.

Akram says the fee increase has delayed his plans to lodge the application, adding another hurdle before he and his wife can begin the process of reuniting in Australia.

For Sarosh Akram, the immediate challenge is to find the extra money he now needs to lodge a partner visa application for his wife. Source: Supplied / Sarosh Akram

Akram's case highlights a broader debate over Australia's partner visa system, now among the most expensive in the developed world, with applicants facing rising fees and lengthy waits, while the government argues the increases are needed to fund migration system reforms.

Paying more, waiting longer

Partner visa applications can be lodged through two pathways: offshore for applicants outside Australia and onshore for applicants already in Australia.

Both pathways involve a two-stage process: eligible applicants first receive a temporary partner visa before becoming eligible for permanent residency at a later stage. The full visa application charge (VAC), however, is paid upfront when the combined application is lodged.

According to the Department of Home Affairs' website, the median processing time for offshore partner visa applications is approximately 16 months, meaning half of the applicants receive a decision within that period. Ninety per cent of applicants receive a decision within 27 months. The data was last updated on 26 June 2026.

Source: SBS News

Those waiting times have become a reality for partner visa sponsors like Ahtesham Altaf.

The 36-year-old lodged his wife's offshore partner visa application in January and has been waiting ever since.

"I applied with the hope that I would get a visa soon, as I was paying quite a higher price compared to other visas, but instead I've been waiting since then," he tells SBS News.

I've tried multiple visa options to bring my wife to Australia, but even her visitor visa application was refused.

Working as a civil engineer in the regional NSW city of Maitland, Altaf moved to Australia in 2023 as a skilled migrant on a permanent visa.

He says he has since spent close to $10,500 on visa fees and medical checks, with no certainty about when his wife will be able to join him.

Ahtesham Altaf lodged his wife's offshore partner visa application in January and has been waiting since then. Source: Supplied / Ahtesham Altaf

Abul Rizvi, former deputy secretary of the immigration department, says cases like Altaf's reflect a "growing" backlog that fee increases alone are unlikely to fix.

The fee increases are generally poor policy.

"The fee increase may marginally slow the application rate , but the backlog is so big and the application rate so much higher than the finalisation rate and the planning level that the backlog will keep growing," Rizvi tells SBS News.

He also raises questions about how visa fee revenue is being used.

"The current political climate means the government can increase the fees to extraordinary levels and it appears not to use the money to clear backlogs without fear of political criticism."

What does the government say?

The government says the increase in VAC is part of wider reforms to the migration system and is intended to support improvements across the migration program.

In an interview with SBS Nepali, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said he did not accept the way the visa fee increase has been characterised, arguing visa fees needed to be considered alongside other costs involved in moving overseas.

"Just remember with the costs as well, anybody who's travelling overseas for an extended period of time has already decided that they've got the cost of an airfare and, you know, the visa fees are, are well below that," he said.

Credit: SBS

Burke acknowledged the importance of partner visas and the personal circumstances behind many applications, but said the government must make decisions across the entire migration system with available resources.

"Every visa category exists because there are benefits to Australia and the sort of country we are if we can fill those positions. And I have to deal with that with the limited resources that we have."

Among the 'highest-cost' partner visa pathways

Rumina Iqbal, a Melbourne-based registered migration agent who has worked with partner visa applications for the past decade, says applicants are paying significantly more for a process where waiting times have remained broadly similar.

While VACs are typically reviewed and adjusted annually, with changes taking effect from 1 July each year as part of the government's standard indexation process, Iqbal says this year's increases for some visa categories are unprecedented and exceed what would ordinarily be expected from CPI-linked indexation.

Every year, there is an increase in the partner visa fee, but it was never this much. This time, it's huge.

Australia's partner visa cost is among the highest compared with similar family migration pathways in several countries. The United Kingdom's spouse visa, applied for from outside the country, costs about $3,942, while New Zealand's Partner of a New Zealander Resident Visa costs about $4,438.

By comparison, a standard Canadian spousal sponsorship costs about $1,364 in government fees, while the United States pathway costs around $1,872 to 1,955.

The fee varies across countries because some include the medical examination and other miscellaneous charges in the total upfront cost.

Migration agent Rumina Iqbal says partner visa applicants are paying a lot more for a process where waiting times have remained largely similar. Source: Supplied / Rumina Iqbal

While migration systems and eligibility requirements vary between countries, Iqbal says the comparisons show the financial burden faced by Australian partner visa applicants.

"When we look at the price tag, it's one of the highest in the developed world, with such long waiting times," she says.

She says the financial pressure extends beyond the initial payment, as partner visa application fees are generally non-refundable.

"If your relationship ends, then, other than in very limited circumstances, you might not be able to get your visa fee back," she says, noting that family violence and partner death are among the few exceptions.

Iqbal says applicants need to carefully consider the financial commitment before lodging, as the cost can add to the pressure during an already lengthy process.

She says the government could reduce that stress by allowing applicants to split the payment across the visa stages rather than paying the full fee upfront.

The cost of waiting

A Department of Home Affairs spokesperson said the government is investing in reforming the migration system through the 2026-27 federal budget, with additional revenue from the VAC increases supporting these reforms alongside other priorities.

The spokesperson said Australia remains an attractive destination, and higher application charges are unlikely to materially affect demand for most visa categories.

They say VACs are often only a small part of an applicant's overall cost to travel to, work in, or live in Australia.

"Migrants come to Australia seeking access to our strong labour market, high quality of life, reliable infrastructure, and stable political climate," the spokesperson told SBS News.

The department also notes that demand for permanent visas continues to exceed the places available under Australia's permanent migration planning levels.

For sponsors like Akram, the challenge is finding the extra money needed just to lodge an application.

For others like Altaf, paying the fee was only the beginning. He is still waiting for the decision that will allow his wife to join him in Australia. Until then, the thousands of dollars spent have secured little more than a place in the queue.

title: Why your super fund's strong run is unlikely to last
text:
IN BRIEF More than 76,000 jobs were created last month, keeping pressure on the Reserve Bank over inflation.

Record avocado production is expected to keep supermarket prices lower for longer.

A rate rise warning amid a strong jobs market, super news for retirees despite a property downturn, and records broken for Australia’s avocado industry.

SBS Finance Editor Ricardo Gonçalves takes a look at three finance news stories of the week and explains how they’ll impact you.

Superannuation funds have delivered another standout year for Australians, but experts say investors shouldn't expect these returns to continue.

Australia's jobs market remains stronger than expected, fuelling speculation the Reserve Bank could raise interest rates again, and avocado lovers have been given some welcome news with prices tipped to stay low.

Don't expect another super year like this
