Australia's superannuation funds have delivered another impressive year, but experts are warning members not to expect these returns every year.

New data from superannuation research firm Chant West shows the median growth fund returned 9.5 per cent over the past financial year, marking four consecutive years of returns above 9 per cent.

Chant West head of superannuation investment Mano Mohankumar told the SBS On the Money podcast that while recent performance has been strong, it's unlikely to continue indefinitely.

Strong international sharemarket gains helped drive returns, with global shares rising more than 25 per cent over the year. Australian shares also posted solid gains of around 6 per cent.

One of the few weaker spots was Australian listed property, which comes as new figures from Domain showed national median house and unit prices recorded their first quarterly decline in more than three years.

Australia's jobs market remains a sticking point for the Reserve Bank

The chance of another interest rate rise increased this week after stronger-than-expected employment figures.

More than 76,000 jobs were created last month, while the unemployment rate held steady at 4.4 per cent because more Australians entered the workforce, pushing the participation rate to a one-year high of 67 per cent.

The participation rate measures the share of working-age Australians who are either employed or actively looking for work. Economists say the increase could reflect ongoing demand for workers or more people seeking employment as cost of living pressures persist.

Citi Australia senior economist Faraz Syed told the SBS On the Money podcast the key concern for the Reserve Bank is whether a tight labour market starts driving wages significantly higher.

The next official inflation figures will be released on Wednesday, ahead of the Reserve Bank's next board meeting on 10 August.

Good news for avocado lovers

If you've noticed cheaper avocados at the supermarket, that trend looks set to continue.

New research from Rabobank found Australian avocado production has rebounded strongly, with both supply and exports expected to reach record highs.

Australian avocado production has rebounded strongly, with both supply and exports expected to reach record highs.

The increase has been driven by expanding orchards and improving yields as newer plantings mature.

While that's welcome news for growers exporting to markets including Hong Kong, Singapore and Malaysia, it's also good news for Australian shoppers, with abundant supply expected to keep retail avocado prices relatively low compared with historical standards.

title: Flaming teacakes, bedazzled unicorns: The Commonwealth Games' surprises unpacked
text:
In brief The Commonwealth Games has opened in Glasgow, Scotland, with a quirky ceremony.

King Charles and Queen Camilla got in on the act, referencing a famous UK sci-fi TV show.

The Head of the Commonwealth emerging from a time-travelling blue box, unicorns prancing on stage, and fire spurting from an oversized teacake.

Those were the scenes at the opening ceremony of the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow on Friday morning.

Victoria was initially meant to host the games, but withdrew in 2023 due to soaring costs.

Glasgow, which previously hosted the event in 2014, stepped in to save it — and brought their finest, most-bedazzled unicorns to mark the occasion.

This year's Commonwealth Games is running on a bare-bones budget, arriving at a time when people have questioned their relevance, particularly following the Victorian government's withdrawal.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

But despite the troubles, Friday's ceremony was a party — with scenes that looked like they could have been plucked from vivid dreams.

King Charles and Queen Camilla walked out of the TARDIS from the iconic British television show, Doctor Who. Source: Getty / Francois Nel

King Charles and Camilla arrive by TARDIS

One of the most unique scenes from Friday morning was the image of King Charles and Queen Camilla emerging from a very large TARDIS — the name for the time machine in the long-running British sci-fi television show, Doctor Who.

Gasps and cheers came from the crowd as the royal couple appeared on a stage that transformed into a magic garden.

Scotland's largest city welcomed able-bodied and para-athletes from 74 competing nations, including a third of Australia's 257-strong team who were part of the procession.

It's not the first time a monarch has appeared at a similar event. For the opening ceremony of the 2012 London Olympics, Queen Elizabeth II appeared to skydive into the stadium alongside Daniel Craig, James Bond-style.

In Glasgow, the UK's new prime minister Andy Burnham was also in attendance, alongside Scotland's First Minister John Swinney and the First Minister of Wales Rhun ap Iorwerth.

Performers took to the stage during the opening on the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. Source: Getty / James Fearn

A party — with unicorns

The opening ceremony traversed through many facets of Glasgow's history and culture, starting with a day in the life of the industrial city, pictured under its famous Glasgow Central Station clock.

The flashmob soon descended into a bizarre fever dream, where dancing unicorns with traffic cones paid tribute to the city's underground club culture.

Dancers wore bedazzled unicorns on their heads. Source: PA / Andrew Milligan

For decades, traffic cones have been regularly placed on an equestrian statue of the Duke of Wellington and remain a symbol of Glaswegians' resistance to authority.

The unicorn is both a nod to the playful tradition and the creature being the national animal of Scotland since the 1300s.

Performers also donned large, shiny star costumes. Source: Getty / Francois Nel

There were also plenty of cameos and performances, including from a range of Scottish celebrities.

Former Doctor Who actor Sylvester McCoy made an appearance, as well as comedian Greg McHugh, cycling legend Sir Chris Hoy, and singers Callum Beattie, KT Tunstall, Tom Walker and Nathan Evans.

King Charles also met Finne, the unicorn mascot representing the 2026 Games. Source: Getty / Aaron Chown

King Charles even had the pleasure of meeting the official mascot for the 2026 Games — a unicorn named Finnie, with a traffic cone for a horn and a pink-and-purple mane.

Loch Ness Monsters and flaming teacakes

Victoria's withdrawal was also referenced throughout the night — with George Black, chair of the Glasgow 2026 organising committee, hailing Scotland's cultural capital for saving the games.

"A city built by people who believe that when something matters, you step forward," Black said on stage.

"When the future of these Games was uncertain, Glasgow didn't ask, 'can we?'

"We asked, "When do we get started?'"

The Loch Ness monster also attended the Glasgow ceremony. Source: Getty / Ross MacDonald

Even Nessie, the Loch Ness Monster, cleared up its schedule to make an appearance.

The creature appeared on a screen before being magically coaxed onto the stage by actor Sam Heughan of Outlander fame and a group of bagpipers.

The ceremony also featured a giant teacake, spurting with pyrotechnics. Source: PA / Andrew Milligan

The finale featured a giant teacake with pyrotechnics flowing from it, taking off from the centre of the stage.

It was a nod to the dancing Teacakes which appeared the last time Glasgow hosted the event in 2014.

Back then, dancers wore costumes representing dessert and national treasure, Tunnock's Tea Cakes — which is a Scottish treat of chocolate-covered marshmallows — and quickly became a worldwide hit.

At the time, a single teacake prop sold at official auctions for over $3,000.

Today's ceremony was held at the Hydro Arena in Glasgow, which fits about 15,000 people, and was the first time a Commonwealth Games opening ceremony was held indoors.

— With reporting by the Australian Associated Press.

title: Police allege Socceroos star tested positive for cocaine after speeding twice
text:
In brief Cristian Volpato switched his allegiance from Italy to Australia just before to the World Cup.

He was stopped twice within hours for speeding, according to police.

Socceroos star Cristian Volpato has allegedly tested positive for cocaine, after police stopped him while speeding over a bridge.

The 22-year-old, who represented Australia at the World Cup, was caught speeding twice overnight, NSW Police said on Friday.

Driving a BMW, Volpato was allegedly clocked at 109 km/h — nearly 50 km/h over the designated speed limit — when police stopped him on Sydney's Anzac Bridge at 1.10am on Friday.

He was subjected to a roadside drug test which allegedly returned a positive result for cocaine, police said in a statement.

A secondary sample of oral fluid was taken for further analysis.

title: An orange wave is breaking over Victoria. Can Labor hold back the populist tide?
text:
No matter who emerges from Labor’s leadership contest, the victor will have to prepare to fight One Nation. This feature has been republished in the wake of Jacinta Allan’s colleagues turning against her.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The hard men and women of the union movement gathered at a conference centre on the edge of Melbourne didn’t entirely believe what they were being told. Kos Samaras, a former Labor Party organiser turned pollster and political consultant, was on his feet, explaining how One Nation, a party which had never won a lower house seat in Victoria, was on track to snatch a dozen at the next state election. In some Labor-held electorates, Pauline Hanson’s lot was Hoovering up 30 per cent of the vote. The room was not entirely convinced. Any union secretary worth their salt knows the mood on the factory floor, in the smoko room, around the teachers’ staff room. They weren’t picking up what Samaras was telling them. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson at a fundraiser in Melbourne on Friday night. Simon Schluter As it turns out, they were right to be sceptical. Samaras didn’t know the half of it. The setting was the annual strategic forum of Victorian Trades Hall Council, the state’s peak body for trade unions, at a venue in Chirnside Park. The date was March, after One Nation had flexed in South Australia, but before Hanson’s party reduced the Liberal and National parties to bit players in the Farrer byelection. What seemed an alarming prediction now appears a gross underestimation of where One Nation is heading. “People thought that 12 seats was maybe a stretch,” Trades Hall secretary Luke Hilakari recalls of the forum. “Now I’m looking at numbers like it could be 30 seats.”

Advertisement

Follow live updates: Jacinta Allan faces leadership threat To put this into context, the Liberal and National parties currently hold 29 seats in Victoria’s Legislative Assembly (lower house). If the revised projections commissioned by Trades Hall are accurate, One Nation will in November become the second-largest party in parliament behind Labor, and the dominant coalition partner within any non-Labor government. As dramatic as this outcome would be, it is only part of the seismic shift we are seeing in Victoria, one mirrored in Donald Trump’s America, in Nigel Farage’s UK and across Western Europe, where populist movements have either replaced or decimated traditional centre-right parties. Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election One Nation entrenched as third force as Victorians adopt ‘drain the swamp’ mentality The Victorian election, the first since One Nation overtook both major parties in popularity, could also produce the next step in Australia’s political upheaval – the emergence of an anti-establishment force capable of taking ground from both the right and the left, and muscling its way onto the government benches. Jim Reed, founder of the Resolve Political Monitor surveys published by The Age, says One Nation has morphed from a protest movement into an agent of change that voters from a broad range of demographics are approaching with positive intent. “The polls are showing One Nation stealing votes from both major parties, not just the right,” he says. Reed’s next survey of Victorian voting intentions will be published on Monday.

Advertisement

Federal One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce declared to 3AW on Friday that his party was now a force that both sides of politics needed to reckon with. “The movement’s on. It’s not an aberration,” he said. When seen this way, the November 28 poll is less a contest between Labor and Liberal than an insider-outsider stoush in which Labor’s biggest fight is against One Nation, the Coalition’s greatest rival is One Nation, and the make-up of parliament will be decided by a kaleidoscope of contests – red versus blue versus orange, not to mention green and teal. Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election Jacinta Allan vows to take up fight against ‘anti-worker’ One Nation A Labor versus Liberal fight for a marginal, mortgage belt seat will seem almost quaint. Back in March, the union leaders left Chirnside Park with another piece of work commissioned by Trades Hall: a 67-page thesis developed by a clever young researcher named Oscar Kaspi-Crutchett, about how the left should fight the far right. Simply titled Antidote, it presents the case that while right-wing populism often begins as a glitch in the centre-right matrix, its “path to power leads through the working class”. This is where the broader labour movement, including the Victorian ALP and the Allan government, wants to take the fight ahead of the election. While the Spring Street echo chamber is preoccupied with speculation about a challenge to Jacinta Allan’s leadership, Hilakari knows Labor faces far bigger questions.

Advertisement

“This is the most progressive state in the nation,” he says. “If One Nation plants their flag here in Victoria, they’re every chance to sweep the nation. This is where the fight is. This is the battleground. If we can’t push them out of Victoria, what’s that going to be like for Queensland, NSW and then the federal election? “We’re running against Pauline Hanson.” Allan this week sought to reframe the contest and sharpen her party’s focus and response to One Nation’s electoral threat. On a crisp winter’s day, she found an hour to slip out of her Treasury Place office, walk with this masthead around Fitzroy Gardens, and share her thoughts about what we are seeing in national and Victorian politics. “What we knew as the old rules of politics don’t exist,” Allan says. “What we are seeing here with the fracturing of mainstream political parties is happening in Victoria, around the country and other parts of the world. Victorian Premier Jacinta Allan says One Nation’s policies will hurt the same working people drawn to its cause. Justin McManus “We are the next big election going around. South Australia was an indicator, and obviously in published polls at a national level and state level around the country, we are seeing the One Nation vote surge. I think One Nation are a risk to working people and families everywhere, and we are the next ones who will be going up against them. That is why you will see me talk a lot about job security, about supporting workers, about helping people.” Allan has raised the spectre of a One Nation-Liberal government. Under this scenario, Hanson, a Queensland senator but with the ultimate authority within One Nation, would have a real and present influence over Victoria’s affairs. Invert the question of how Opposition Leader Jess Wilson would govern if she accepts One Nation as a junior Coalition partner. What would One Nation’s Victorian leader – a position yet to be filled– do as premier?

Advertisement

Either way, the election will break new ground. This is the first state or federal election since One Nation’s revival a decade ago where it is poised to win seats from Labor as well as the Coalition. This didn’t happen in South Australia, where One Nation won four lower house seats off the Liberal Party. It didn’t happen in Farrer, where Labor didn’t contest, and One Nation won a federal seat held by the Coalition since its creation. To find the last time it did, you need to go back to 1998, when the first iteration of One Nation won six seats from Labor and five from the Nationals at the Queensland state election. Hanson says her ultimate aim in Victoria is to remove a long-term Labor administration that has plunged the state into record debt, allowed criminals to infiltrate its Big Build program and overseen record levels of crime. She told a fundraiser event in Melbourne on Friday night she would be willing to partner the Coalition in government to achieve this goal. While opinion is split about whether this is a gift to the Liberal Party or a curse, Allan is clear on what the worst outcome would be: a One Nation-led government. Loading The Liberal Party will, meanwhile, keep pressing the case that if One Nation supporters really want to change the government, the best way is to vote for the Coalition. To understand what the next parliament could look like, let’s return to the Redbridge seat-by-seat modelling Samaras presented to the Trades Hall Council in March, and has since updated. It showed Labor’s seats most likely to be swamped by an orange wave are in outer suburban and semi-rural areas, like Melton and Sydenham in Melbourne’s west and Pakenham, Bass and Hastings in the south-east. These are areas on the front line of the population debate that Hanson has sought to exploit as she blames “mass immigration” for overburdened roads, trains, schools and hospitals.

Advertisement

They also have a higher proportion of people who are not university educated and who are either production workers, service workers or small business owners. Kaspi-Crutchett identifies these three groups as having changeable political allegiances. “These communities are more exposed to economic shocks and consequently exhibit outsized discontent with the status quo,” he says in Antidote. Wherever the far-right has achieved critical mass, it has done so by winning over significant portions of these occupational groups, Kaspi-Crutchett says. The urban fringe is also a dangerous place for the Liberal Party, with similar seats, such as Berwick (the electorate held by former leader Brad Battin), Croydon and Evelyn (which includes Chirnside Park) also in play. The electoral map for the Nationals is even more bleak because One Nation was already resonating with some regional voters at the 2022 state election. Samaras’ research shows seats such as Murray Plains, Gippsland East, Shepparton and Euroa are at risk of turning orange. Samaras, who declined to discuss his confidential modelling, says that on published polling results, the Nationals could lose all their seats. But he adds an important caveat: “If you were going to pick a group of National MPs who could defend their seats because of who they are, I would pick the Victorians.” Nationals leader Danny O’Brien says that at the last election, voters elected four new National MPs, including two who replaced independents. “Our great party has been written off many times in our 110-year history, but we have always prevailed because country people want a party that looks out for them and fights for their fair share,” he says. Publican Andrew Lethlean is trying to win Jacinta Allan’s seat of Bendigo East for the Nationals this November. Penny Stephens The nuclear scenario, one canvassed by a Labor source, is that One Nation could wipe all established parties off Victoria’s regional and rural map. Speaking on the condition of anonymity, the source said the outlook for Labor had deteriorated from bad to catastrophic. If this situation is realised, then Allan’s seat of Bendigo East is squarely in the One Nation firing line. This comes on top of a well-planned Nationals challenge by Andrew Lethlean, a publican who took Labor’s overlapping federal seat of Bendigo to the brink of defeat in last year’s federal election. On the desk of his Trades Hall office, Hilakari has an electoral map which, with each new input of data, he colours with shades of orange, blue, red and green. The state of Victoria already resembles a tequila sunset, with One Nation’s putative seats stretching from the edge of Melbourne to the NSW border. Trades Hall secretary Luke Hilakari. Simon Schluter There was a view among Labor, one expressed not long ago, that One Nation and the Liberals would devour one another, leaving the ALP as the only party capable of forming government. This has now been replaced by a growing sense of despair about what to do with a problem like Pauline. A frustrated party official says: “We have a woman who is backed by billionaires, who does not vote for increases in the minimum wage or the pension, who says that people are lazy and don’t want to work, and somehow she is the champion of the working class.” How Victoria – where Labor has governed for all but four years this century – arrived at this place is also a live debate. Kaspi-Crutchett traces the economic and social forces that tilled the soil for Hanson, such as the declining share of the economy paid to workers, growing disparities in the distribution of wealth, and the bleak outlook confronting younger Australians witnessing the disappearance of entry-level jobs and prohibitive house prices. An Essential poll published in the lead-up to the 2025 federal election suggests that even though Labor voters backed in the Albanese government, they weren’t in a good place. According to the survey, only 16 per cent of Labor voters believed the political system was working well, and most felt Australia was on the wrong track. Not many of them will put much weight on this story – only 11 per cent trusted the mainstream media to report accurately. Related Article Opinion

One Nation Like Trump, Hanson’s rise is beyond politics. That’s why she’ll be hard to stop Peter Hartcher Political and international editor Kaspi-Crutchett also presents some uniquely Victorian factors which help explain One Nation’s sudden appeal, noting the COVID-19 experience and particularly the 262 days Melbourne spent in lockdown “turbocharged both the scale and intensity of far-right political activity in the state”. Lydia Khalil and Joshua Roose, experts on extremism, described the anti-lockdown movement in a 2023 paper as “a wide array of actors, including anti-vaxxers, religious communities, wellness influencers, QAnon and other conspiracists, sovereign citizens, and known Australian far-right actors and influencers” who converged alongside ordinary citizens to protest against vaccine mandates and social restrictions. From this unlikely cluster of bedfellows, a cohesive movement formed. Labor knows it is both inaccurate and counterproductive to dismiss One Nation supporters as racist or conspiratorial cranks. Instead, the party’s state and federal headquarters are directing its MPs, including Allan, to shift the argument to what a Labor government can do for working people and what One Nation won’t. That shift has begun, but the hour is late. In a little over five months, Victorians go to the polls for one of the most consequential elections in the state’s history. At least Labor now knows who it is fighting. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. Sign up for our Morning Edition newsletter.

text:

Key points THEATRE: Melbourne Theatre Company’s Uncle Vanya offers up sardonic one-liners

MUSIC: ACO’s From Winter’s Stillness is an edgy musical hybrid

THEATRE

Uncle Vanya ★★★★

Melbourne Theatre Company, Arts Centre Melbourne, until August 22 It’s a rare and charming thing to see Uncle Vanya done in period dress, as it is in Anne-Louise Sarks’ latest production for the MTC, on a splendid set that evokes a crumbling provincial estate in the last decade of the 19th century. Singling out actors for praise in Chekhov may be inevitable but always feels like a betrayal. Pia Johnson Contemporary Chekhovian performance tends to modernise, reframe, relocate. It’s as if we wanted to fire a bullet at the past – an exercise in futility, as Vanya himself discovers twice. Time doesn’t work that way. Playwright Joanna Murray-Smith believes (rightly) that such modernising is unnecessary in a good Chekhov production. Her Vanya adaptation gives a light textual massage for clarity, to draw out the comedy and update the vernacular.

Advertisement

As you’d expect from Murray-Smith, the sardonic one-liners are mercilessly sharp, and characters slip in words like “f---wit” and “bonking”, while being aware enough to admit that, well, “No one says ‘bonking’ any more.” Beyond that and the sound design – the Violent Femmes’ Add It Up doesn’t feel appropriate to the general vibe – it’s a faithful, lightly periodised production and an excellent intro to Chekhovian tragicomedy. It’s a rare and charming thing to see Uncle Vanya done in period dress. Pia Johnson Singling out actors for praise in Chekhov may be inevitable but always feels like a betrayal. Star turns can damage the delicate ensemble performance required to portray human contingency and incompleteness, and on that level this production sometimes feels more like a collection of exquisitely rendered individual performances – the human equivalent of the autumn leaves falling in its opening scene – than a true ensemble piece. There’s still much to admire. Sarks emphasises humiliation as key to whatever self-awareness the characters might avoid or achieve, and the romantic excruciations (everyone is famously in love with the wrong person) are beautifully done.

Advertisement

Philippa Northeast invests the role of Sonya with girlish comedy, throwing herself at Astrov (Fayssal Bazzi) with the full cringe of unrequited infatuation, while the charismatic doctor and environmentalist – whose dashing good looks and vaulting idealism coexist with burnout and radical disillusionment and emotional disconnection – seduces the beautiful young Yelena (Catherine Văn-Davies) with a palpable edge of self-loathing. Daniel Henshall’s Vanya is a veritable humiliation magnet. It’s a notably unsympathetic portrayal. A beta male to the core, this Vanya is an intensely pathetic figure who projects his own inadequacies onto his brother-in-law, the Professor (played in a nimble, lightly drawn lampoon of intellectual pomposity by Shaun Micallef) even as he makes embarrassing moves on the Professor’s young wife and pours blatant misogyny over everyone, including his would-be suffragist mother (Carolyn Bock). Daniel Henshall’s Vanya is a veritable humiliation magnet. Pia Johnson Vanya might feel like a minor character in his own life, but it’s Chekhov’s actual minor characters who cope best with humiliation. The longsuffering Waffles (Don Bridges) is warmly and affectionately conveyed, as is the stolidity of the pipe-smoking Nanny (Evelyn Krape). They’re both gloriously unselfconscious – one antidote to humiliation – and such brief moments of freedom are among the production’s most elevating, including a poignant scene where Sonya and Yelena are together, chatting and drinking and playing together like sisters, away from all the fuss the men are causing.

Advertisement

On opening night, some performances didn’t seem entirely bedded down. Henshall appeared to go dry at one point – a metatheatrical humiliation that seemed apposite, in context – but it might be the consistency of dramatic tempo that’s the biggest niggle. Related Article Streaming It may offend the book’s rusted-on fans, but this series should be approached with an open mind How we experience time, and how we handle futility and ennui, are among Chekhov’s main themes, and the one time I saw the Russians perform Vanya – by the Maly Drama Theatre of St Petersburg in 2007 – they brazenly manipulated the elastic temporal quality of theatre. (That production went for over three hours, dared the audience to be bored, and unfolded as inescapably as if it were being performed inside a black hole.) It would be churlish – maybe even Vanya-like – to complain that the audience wasn’t bored enough, though, and if it doesn’t quite deliver the epiphany into the human condition you get from the highest level of Chekhovian performance, this production’s desire to entertain is a no less crucial element of the drama. After all, Chekhov’s characters are always performing to allay such tedium, or at least give it form. And that aspect of being human is as timeless as it gets.

Reviewed by Cameron Woodhead

Advertisement

MUSIC

From Winter’s Stillness ★★★★

Australian Chamber Orchestra, Hamer Hall, until July 27 What do you get when you cross the Australian Chamber Orchestra with a jazz trumpeter and a Norwegian trio of female voices specialising in medieval, Nordic folk and contemporary music? Trumpeter Arve Henriksen performs is performing with the Australian Chamber Orchestra. Julia Marie Naglestad Well, certainly an edgy musical hybrid pushing the boundaries of “classical” programming, delighting intrepid listeners and probably perplexing others. The perplexity was heightened because printed programs only became available at interval, leaving most of the audience adrift in the unusual musical terrain of the first half. Trumpeter Arve Henriksen’s The Plume of Ash and Acceptance set a reflective mood, contrasted by the indefatigable minimalism of Terry Riley’s Half Wolf Dances Mad in the Moonlight.

Advertisement

Estonian composer Tõnu Kõrvits’ Bells, written for Henriksen and Trio Mediæval (singers Anna Maria Friman, Ditte Marie Bræin and Jorunn Lovise Husan), exerted a mesmeric quality that sat well alongside Academy Award-winning Icelandic composer Hildur Guðnadóttir’s Time and Water (especially written for this tour). Related Article ★★★★★

Melbourne live reviews It took 48 years, but this show has finally made it to Melbourne. It was worth the wait This Little Child, a sad traditional Norwegian song preceded Icelandic band Sigur Ros’ Fljótavik, an ideal vehicle for Hendriksen, whose unique, mellow tone unfurled over the music’s ground bass. In the second half, movements of Soviet composer Alfred Schnittke’s Concerto Grosso No.1 were interleaved with jazz-infused musings on Nordic chant and folk material. Schnittke’s iconoclasm is mercifully leavened with a generous sense of humour. Soloists Richard Tognetti and Satu Vänskä met the outrageous technical demands with aplomb, aided by customarily fine support from the rest of the ACO.

Advertisement

Using a cyclorama against which performers were either silhouetted or spotlit, head of lighting Joe Cox created a welcoming, unifying mood across this diverse program. Trio Mediæval’s limpid vocal quality was a delight throughout and together with flashes of brilliance from Henriksen, this eclectic experience was bound to get listeners talking – presumably as the ACO intended.

Barkly Rare Earths has sent the first batch of samples from its 10,000-metre resource expansion drill campaign to the laboratory, a key step in its push to grow its already significant rare earths inventory at its flagship Barkly project in the Northern Territory. The campaign is designed to test for shallow mineralisation around the company’s existing 40-million-tonne inferred mineral resource, which grades an impressive 2100 parts per million (ppm) total rare earth oxides (TREO). Barkly Rare Earths Managing Director, Craig Wright, inspects laboratory sample preparation equipment at the ALS laboratory in Brisbane to be used for samples from the company’s 10,000m NT drilling campaign. Previous drilling between these two areas intersected rare earths hinting at the potential for significant lateral expansion across the intervening 20-kilometre corridor. Barkly has defined an exploration target that gives a sense of the scale it is chasing. It ranges from 200 million to 1 billion tonnes at a grade of between 1600 and 1900 ppm TREO. If the company can get anywhere near even the lower end of that range, it could potentially be sitting on a globally significant deposit.

Advertisement

‘This is where the campaign moves from metres drilled to assay results.’ Barkly Rare Earths managing director Craig Wright The company has adopted a two-pronged strategy for the campaign. The early stage will involve drilling a series of deeper, 60-metre holes to provide a stronger geological framework for the current deposit. The rig will then move on to the main event, a pattern of up to 400 shallow holes averaging just 25 metres deep targeting an area dubbed the Immediate Zone. This Immediate Zone sits within an underexplored 20-kilometre corridor connecting the two resource areas with the first samples from the program having already arrived at the ALS lab in Brisbane for analysis. Barkly Rare Earths managing director Craig Wright said: “The objective is clear, test the shallow mineralisation around our existing 40 Mt Inferred Resource and generate the data intended to support a resource update later this year.” Barkly says what makes the project compelling is not just the potential scale but the high proportion of valuable magnet rare earth oxides which account for 34 per cent of the total resource. These are the elements critical for manufacturing high-strength magnets used in everything from electric vehicles to wind turbines.

Advertisement

Critically, initial test work has yielded low levels of uranium and thorium – both unwanted elements which can often complicate processing. In another notable milestone leaching tests achieved a 74 per cent extraction rate for magnet rare earths with early-stage beneficiation work producing a mineral concentrate grading a hefty 29,000 ppm TREO. Additionally, Barkly is armed with two recent grants of $115,000 each awarded under the Northern Territory’s highly regarded Geophysics and Drilling Collaborations program. And while the company’s main game is its rare earths project, it also holds the Buntine project in the Northern Territory where it is chasing green fields base metals. Notably, it says the project’s geology at Buntine is the same as the rocks that host the world-class McArthur River lead-zinc deposit with polymetallic mineralisation already having been identified along a nine-kilometre strike length. Initial rock chipping has returned grades of up to one per cent lead, 1760 ppm cobalt and 7100 ppm nickel. Gateway Mining has again stretched the boundaries of its rapidly emerging Cowza gold discovery, adding another kilometre of high-grade strike to deliver an impressive 3.5-kilometre mineralised system at its Yandal gold project in Western Australia. The latest wide-spaced air-core drilling has confirmed strong continuity of gold mineralisation along every drill traverse completed to date, with standout intercepts including 4 metres grading 11.1 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 72m, 8m at 3.1g/t gold from 76m and 4m at 3.3g/t gold from 80m. Air-core drilling at Gateway Mining’s Yandal gold project in Western Australia, where ongoing drilling continues to expand the rapidly growing Cowza gold discovery. Barely a week after tripling the strike to 2.5 kilometres, Gateway has already pushed Cowza another kilometre farther, reinforcing the view that the discovery is still in rapid growth mode. Cowza’s strike is expanding almost as quickly as Gateway can drill it. Cowza sits on the contact between mafic and intermediate volcanic rocks within a 4.5km structural corridor showing strong demagnetisation, shearing and alteration – all classic hallmarks of a fertile gold system. Management believes the consistency of the geological signatures presents as a blueprint for further discoveries with the prospect of contacts and major regional shears repeatedly combining to host additional gold mineralisation across the project.

‘The growing body of evidence suggests Cowza has the potential to become a significant gold discovery within the Yandal Project.’ Gateway Mining chief executive officer Richard Pugh Adding to the intrigue, a further 1km of drilling north of the current assay area has already intersected the same favourable shearing, veining and alteration, suggesting the discovery could continue its march northwards. Assays for those holes are pending as Gateway continues testing extensions to the rapidly growing system. Gateway Mining chief executive officer Richard Pugh said: “The rapid growth of the Cowza system continues to exceed expectations, with gold mineralisation now defined over an impressive 3.5 kilometre strike length and remaining open in multiple directions.” Gateway is now stepping on the accelerator. A second reverse-circulation (RC) rig is arriving on site this week and will be dedicated entirely to Cowza as the company moves to define the rapidly expanding scale and continuity of the fresh-rock mineralisation. The first RC rig is already drilling at the Haflinger discovery, further north within the project area. Cowza has already evolved from an encouraging aircore anomaly into one of the fastest-growing discoveries in Gateway’s Yandal portfolio. Stop press. I’ve got exciting news. We finally have an Australian-made non-alcoholic ‘wine’ that tastes like wine. Surprisingly, it took a beer brewer to nail it. I had high but cautious expectations when I caught wind that Sydney-based non-alc beer gurus Heaps Normal were releasing a High Hopes Prosecco. Since launching in July 2020, co-founder Ben Holdstock and his team raised the non-alc bar with their XPA, IPA, Lager, and Stout. But wine is a different beast. Heaps Normal have High Hopes for the new sparkling. Globally, few get it right, and the reason is simple. Alcohol literally brings a lot to the table. It provides mouthfeel and texture, palate weight, a warming sensation or heat, and psychological effects.

Advertisement

“When you take the ethanol out of wine, you lose a lot,” says Dr Wes Pearson, research scientist at the Australian Wine Research Institute (AWRI). The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up “Ethanol is a very unique compound, and there really isn’t much else like it chemically. When you remove that from wine, you’re left with something that is thin and acidic, has a watery feel and no longer resembles any concept of traditional wine.” So how did a self-proclaimed disruptive business with a non-alc beer background like Heaps Normal crack the code? Lots of research. Rage without alcohol with High Hopes. The sparkling wine took 18 months to develop, in collaboration with the Australian Wine Research Institute (AWRI), and is made with 100 per cent grapes sourced from Hilltops in NSW. Throughout the process, Heaps Normal head of wine, Ned Brooks, engaged with winemakers, bartenders and organic chemists at the AWRI’s No-Low Wine Research Centre.

“I did a bit of a deep dive into the category and tasted a lot,” Brooks says. “It always felt like people were making non-alcoholic wines just to fill a category in their range. There weren’t many who were actually trying to build a drink that was worthy of drinking.” While Australia has some impressive NoLo wine alternatives, the stuff made with grapes didn’t really cut it. Heaps Normal founders Andy Miller, Ben Holdstock and Peter Brennan. “In Australia, it felt like there was a method and no one really deviated from the method which was de-alkalise, add grape concentrate, add flavours, add colours, and add thickener,” Brooks says. “It seemed as if it was a bit of an easy answer, and no one was really willing to think outside the box and try and see what else they could come up with.”

Advertisement

There are some exceptions.



“Edenvale is exclusively a non-alcoholic wine producer, and there are a number of German, American and French producers that are exclusively non-alcoholic as well.” Edenvale is another non-alc prosecco maker. Dr Pearson said Heaps Normal’s approach to product development was “very clever”. “I think they have the benefit of creating products in this space without what I would almost call the ‘burden’ of having a wine background,” he says. “As a beer company, they aren’t obliged to make a product that is a replacement product for traditional wine, as their customers aren’t traditional wine drinkers. They just have to make a product that tastes good, and works for the occasions that their non-alc beer products are being consumed at.”

Advertisement

The wine is produced in-house. High Hopes is one out of the box. “In this instance, it was basically rethinking the whole process,” Brooks says. Not just the alkalization side, but even the harvest, the grape variety, when we’re picking [the grapes] and what we’re achieving in each step in the winemaking process, as opposed to it being an afterthought.” “I thought, ‘Can I make something that’s dry – kind of an aperitif style that’s going to suit somebody who wants to have it with oysters, rather than something that feels like sweet green bubbles?’” Ned Brooks, Heaps Normal head of wine Brooks’ wine background includes working in wineries, hospitality, retail and wholesale. He wanted to make something that worked as a standalone drink as well as with food.



“Prosecco as a category is so broad in the styles,” he says. “I thought, ‘Can I make something that’s dry – kind of an aperitif style that is going to suit somebody who wants to have it with oysters, rather than something that feels like sweet green bubbles?’”

As for what’s next for Heaps Normal, there are positive signs for those thirsty for a new, non-alc still wine option, too. “We’re currently working through the process of research and development on a still product”, says Brooks. “I don’t really have a date or anything like that, but we are trying to figure that out.” High Hopes from Heaps Normal The verdict My verdict on the Heaps Normal High Hopes Prosecco? It’s excellent. Smashing, even. It actually tastes like Prosecco. There are lashings of lemon, life-affirming fizz, head-snapping acidic twang, depth of flavour, and bubbles that last the distance.

A local upsizer paid $2 million for a small semi in Balmain after the vendor dropped their reserve by $100,000 at auction on Saturday. The two-bedder with stained glass, iron lacework, a leafy courtyard and upstairs balcony at 15 Gladstone Street had clear views across the city, including the Sydney Harbour Bridge. The property was one of 564 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney last week. By Saturday evening, Domain Group had recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 53 per cent from 311 reported results throughout the week, while 93 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. Three parties registered to bid on the Federation-era property with a $2 million guide. All were young couples or families, but only one made an offer, opening the auction at $1.9 million.

The next bid was a vendor bid of $2 million, then the opening bidder asked the auctioneer if they could match the vendor bid. This was accepted. Related Article Auctions First home buyers pay $2.04m for renovated Sydney house as market drops The vendor then agreed to adjust their reserve of $2.1 million, and it sold under the hammer for $2 million. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. Selling agent Richard Baini of Richard Matthews Real Estate said the street was full of onlookers: “The crowd was easily over 100 people.”

“There’s a lot more buyer confidence coming back into the market,” Baini said. “They’ve gone and reassessed their financial position with their brokers and banks, and the buyers are back out looking and buying again.” The vendor is moving out of Sydney. The two-bedroom, top-floor apartment at 8/401 Marrickville Road drew four registrations. Three took part, and all were first home buyers.

Richardson & Wrench’s Aris Dendrinos noted uncertainty in the market. “It’s not a market of fear. It’s a market of uncertainty, and it’s the worst market because when people are fearful, they act. When they’re uncertain, they don’t act,” he said.

“People can panic buy, and people can panic sell because they’re fearful. They want to get their money. They want to move on and do the next thing. But when they’re uncertain, they don’t do much.” The deceased estate last traded for $158,000 in 1994, records show. In Sydney’s south-west, a three-bedroom property drew the interest of three builders who registered at auction. The Carramar block at 107 Mitchell Street was guided at $1 million. title: Trump’s America is sinking as his war on the world sputters
text:

BusinessThe economyTrade wars Opinion Trump’s America is sinking as his war on the world sputters Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist July 27, 2026 — 11:59am

July 27, 2026 — 11:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Donald Trump keeps trying to build his tariff wall, but each time the wall is lower and built on narrower footings. When Trump announced his “Liberation Day” tariffs in April last year, they were expected to raise somewhere between $US1.5 trillion and $US2 trillion ($2.2 trillion to $2.9 trillion) over the next decade. Donald Trump has repeatedly sent conflicting signals about his plans for the Hormuz Strait. Getty Images Those tariffs, of course, got struck out by the US Supreme Court in February, forcing the Trump administration to come up with a replacement, which it did. As a temporary measure, using a section of the Trade Act with a ceiling rate of 15 per cent and forced expiry after 150 days, it imposed a 10 per cent duty on all imports that would raise about $US35 billion while it constructed a permanent replacement.

Advertisement

Those interim tariffs expired last Friday morning and were immediately replaced with a tariff of either 10 per cent or 12.5 per cent on 99.4 per cent of all goods imported to the US, other than those the administration explicitly excepted or where there is a different tariff regime in place, like the 50 per cent duty on imports of steel and aluminium. Related Article Trade As Trump’s new tariffs loom, Australian exporters clamour for carveouts The latest tariffs have supposedly been imposed because all of America’s trading partners, including Australia, have failed to sufficiently crack down on the use of forced labour. In reality, they are the latest attempt to recreate the revenue stream, and the barrier to imports, ruled illegal by the Supreme Court. Thanks to the Supreme Court, the revenue that was collected by the Liberation Day tariffs – more than $US160 billion – has to be refunded, though the administration has done what it can to slow the process and reduce the amount it must return. It has so far, however, paid back more than $US80 billion of the revenue it collected. Last month, the US government’s revenue from customs duties was negative to the tune of $US25.6 billion, after refunds virtually matched receipts in May.

Advertisement

Those tariffs that were supposed to be the interim measure while the administration developed its new permanent replacement for the one knocked out by the Supreme Court will have raised an estimated $US35 billion. The US Court of International Trade has, however, deemed those tariffs illegal too. If that ruling holds up under appeal, that revenue will also have to be refunded. America’s finances are parlous – and deteriorating. Bloomberg Some of the small businesses that successfully challenged the Liberation Day tariffs, and the lawyers who represented them, were involved in the action against the interim tariffs and have already filed a lawsuit against the new duty regime imposed last week. While the section of the Trade Act (Section 301) that the administration is using has been tried and tested and has held up in the courts previously, the sham pretext of inaction against forced labour being used to try to reproduce a global tariff regime to replace the one the Supreme Court declared illegal makes it vulnerable. Under the US Constitution, only Congress has the power to apply universal tariffs.

Advertisement

Related Article Opinion

Trump's White House Trump is back announcing a 2028 presidential bid. It’s not a joke Cory Alpert Former White House staffer Trump plans to use the same section of the Trade Act to impose even more tariffs, with the administration to argue that they are warranted in response to other nations’ trade measures that it deems discriminatory to American businesses. Even if the tariffs imposed last week do hold up under court scrutiny, they are – as revenue raisers – a poor substitute for the Liberation Day tariffs. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB) had a look at the new tariffs last week, along with other country-specific tariffs that Trump announced would be imposed on Canada and Brazil (apparently for their lack of deference to him). The CRFB estimated that the Supreme Court ruling would cost the US government about $US1.7 trillion of revenue it would otherwise have collected over the next decade.

Advertisement

The new universal tariffs, with a lower average rate and far more exclusions (to try to moderate their inflationary effects on consumer prices) would, it said, raise about $US900 billion over a decade and those on Canada and Brazil more than $US50 billion between them – so about $US950 billion in total. That’s only about 56 per cent of the revenue forgone as a result of the Supreme Court’s ruling and, in the context of total US government revenues of more than $US5.6 trillion a year (or the “Department of Wars’ $US1.5 trillion budget request) almost immaterial. Tariff revenues, if they don’t evaporate as a result of the continuing legal actions, aren’t going to solve America’s debt and deficit problems; indeed, they are more likely to exacerbate them because they raise the inflation rate and subtract from economic activity. Whatever Trump and his officials might believe, or at least say, his tariffs are a tax on US businesses and households. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York has calculated that about 90 per cent of their cost is absorbed by domestic businesses and consumers. Loading

Advertisement

The tariffs cost jobs, add up to 70 basis points to the inflation rate and subtract about 0.2 percentage points from US GDP, along with the damage they do to the global economy. There is a view that, whatever tariff revenue the Supreme Court leaves intact will last beyond the point where Trump departs the White House, with Congress, regardless of the party in control, unlikely to voluntarily abandon a revenue stream, albeit one that is a regressive tax on consumers. That’s because America’s finances are parlous, and deteriorating. Trump added $US7.8 trillion to the national debt in his first term, and Joe Biden another $US8 trillion, though both those presidencies were coloured by massive pandemic-driven spending. So far in this term – without a pandemic – Trump has added another $US3.2 trillion, raising gross federal government debt to $US39.3 trillion, or about 125 per cent of US GDP.

Advertisement

The interest bill on that debt is more than $US1 trillion and is rising sharply, influenced significantly by Trump’s policies. Whatever Trump and his officials might believe, or at least say, his tariffs are a tax on US businesses and households. The tariffs, and the war in the Middle East particularly, have pushed up the US inflation rate and have had a marked impact on bond yields. On February 27, the day before the US and Israel attacked Iran, the US 10-year bond yield was 3.94 per cent. Today it is 4.68 per cent. The two-year yield was 3.38 per cent. Now it is 4.33 per cent. With the US Treasury, over several administrations, increasingly raising debt of shorter duration because it was the cheapest segment of the yield curve, about a third of all existing US government debt on issue has to be refinanced this year.

Advertisement

Those higher yields on its bonds mean a government interest bill that already tops a trillion dollars can only increase – relatively minor movement in bond yields can add tens of billions, if not hundreds of billions, to the annual interest bill. Related Article Updated

Trade ‘Economic neanderthal’: Experts warn Trump’s tariff crusade risks global recession Trump may, perhaps, believe that other countries are paying large amounts of cash into his Treasury’s coffers, but they aren’t – and the amounts now involved, assuming he can retain them, aren’t material enough to blunt the impact his profligacy will have on the fiscal legacy he will leave his successors, and US taxpayers. For the Chiefs, who have become too big to fail, signing Lomax is a smart play – he’s high-profile, he’s an Origin player, and he’s still only 26 – and another sign of the club’s lust for immediate, up-front success while building its long-term Marshall Plan for Pacific domination. Doueihi or don’t he? In a curious juxtaposition of events leading into the weekend, there was speculation about Latrell Mitchell and Tom Trbojevic having their pay reduced because of how many matches they miss with injury, while the Tigers’ Adam Doueihi, who has received many months’ worth of paid injury time in his career, chose not to play at all if selected at lock. And on the other hand, you had a first-grader deciding against playing because (his version reportedly) he wanted to highlight “issues” within the club. Wayne Bennett said, rightly, that docking injured players’ pay was a ridiculous idea. It is at complete odds with rugby league’s DNA as a sport aligned with the rise of the labour movement. In a fair system, a worker is not penalised for bad luck. A crestfallen Tom Trbojevic comes off injured against the Gold Coast. Fox Sports But docking the pay of a worker who decides not to turn up? Hmm. In his press conference after the Tigers’ loss to Canberra, coach Benji Marshall walked on eggshells. Then, when questioned about whether a voluntary non-player (Doueihi) deserved his pay, Marshall said: “We’re also in a world where if you don’t feel mentally right to play, you can’t make him play. It’s tough, we’re men, we have feelings, we’re in a day and age where you need to express those feelings, and he did.” Let’s just say Doueihi was allowed a week of paid compassionate leave. Fainu comeback too much even for rugby league “Jailed ex-Manly hooker wanted to play league wearing an ankle bracelet” is not only the best rugby league headline of 2026 but the most rugby league headline of 2026. Manase Fainu was, in 2019, a very promising NRL hooker for Manly and a linchpin of the club’s plans to build a premiership-winning team around the Fainu and Trbojevic families.

It all came unstuck when Manase attacked someone at a Mormon church dance with a knife he pulled out of the sling he was wearing for an injured shoulder (the story kept getting more and more rugby league). Then Manly Sea Eagles hooker Manase Fainu outside court in 2022. Rhett Wyman Now on weekend release after serving his custodial sentence, Fainu has recently applied to play A grade for the Alexandria Rovers. The NSWRL knocked him back on several grounds, including the risk of him causing an injury with his ankle bracelet. A donk on the head from a heavy-duty, impact-resistant polycarbonate GPS device would be a novel excuse for missing a tackle. You’d have thought Corrective Services could easily trace Fainu without the bracelet while he was on the field, but we don’t make the rules.

Russell Packer set a precedent for returning to the NRL in 2016 after serving a prison term for assault, and ARL Commission chairman Peter V’landys is known to like redemption stories on the scale of Greek mythology. But in today’s NRL, a Manase Fainu comeback would require more twists and unlikely favours from the gods than Odysseus’ comeback from Troy. Christmas in July Cronulla are playing better than anyone in the NRL, which makes them the premiers if the grand final was in July. Related Article Manly 12 Cronulla 48

Match report Sharks savaging leaves Sea Eagles’ finals hopes in free fall Checking the NRL casualty list, Cronulla are also the one club with a virtually empty injury ward, only Tom Hazelton being out of action for the weekend.

The Sharks would be the envy of Newcastle, who have just lost the Dylans, Brown and Lucas, for the season and Kalyn Ponga for weeks. Melbourne are without Cameron Munster and Harry Grant among others, North Queensland Tom Dearden, the Dolphins Isaiya Katoa and Souths and Manly have the NRL’s longest casualty lists. As the finals approach, it will be better to be lucky than good.

title: First home buyer gets discount on $722,500 North Melbourne three-bedder

A first home buyer paid $722,500 for an updated three-bedroom apartment in North Melbourne at auction on Saturday, using the federal government’s 5 per cent deposit scheme, after the vendor cut their reserve to sell. Three parties registered to bid for the well-presented home with a balcony and leafy outlook at 5/55 Haines Street, although one didn’t turn up. The property was one of 692 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne last week. By Saturday evening, Domain Group had recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 55 per cent from 464 reported results throughout the week, while 94 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. Two potential buyers arrived for the auction of the North Melbourne apartment, which was on a stratum title, which means each owner in the building has a title to their apartment but holds shares in a company that manages common areas, instead of an owners corporation.

Advertisement

The buyer made a genuine bid of $690,000, below the price guide of $700,000 to $730,000. Related Article Auctions Malvern bungalow sells for $2.66m to buyer who wants to tear it down With no further offers, the home was passed in. The reserve had been $735,000 but the buyer and vendors reached an agreement in post-auction negotiations. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. Jellis Craig Fitzroy selling agent Trevor Gange said the vendors live in New Zealand and no longer require the property, which was recently rented.

Advertisement

Interest in the home was largely from first home buyers, except for one investor who didn’t turn up, Gange said. “It is still a challenging market. There are still deals being done,” he said. “Buyers feel like they have more power. “It is a great market to buy in. There is always people who want to sell, and to buy in a challenging market is better than to buy in a rising market.” An unliveable East Melbourne fixer-upper sold for $2 million, well above its reserve price of $1,625,000.

Advertisement

Related Article Auctions Downsizer cries with joy as she wins $866,000 northern Melbourne home The three-bedroom terrace at 146 Simpson Street was listed with a price guide of between $1.55 million and $1.65 million. Four parties bid, starting from $1.4 million, in $50,000 increments to the bottom of the price guide. Then the stride shortened to a mix of $10,000 and $5000 offers, and two parties fought it out over the last $300,000. Ray White CRE’s Toby Campbell described the sale as a “brilliant result” after the home was in one family for 85 years.

Advertisement

“It was above their wildest hopes,” Campbell said. “The house is totally unlivable. You can’t move in. Some of the floors are collapsed.” Interest came mostly from parties looking to renovate the home themselves, Campbell said, and they were attracted to the single-level layout in a sought-after suburb. One builder-developer bid. The buyers are a couple who intend to renovate but are unsure if they would move in or sell it, Campbell said. He estimated it would need $1 million in renovation works to make it “liveable” and $1.5 million spent to make it “nice”.

Advertisement

In Melbourne’s west, a family paid $858,000 to upsize to a five-bedroom house in Hoppers Crossing. The well-presented home at 41 Birchwood Boulevard was listed with a price guide of $790,000 to $850,000. The reserve was $840,000. Ray White Hoppers Crossing principal director Shahid Khan said the home didn’t sell when it was previously offered to the market. But after some updates, such as rendering and work on the gutters, and a relaunch, the home sold within 25 days. Khan said some buyers worried that small issues could have major costs to fix, but the refurbishments allayed those concerns.

Advertisement

Related Article Property prices Meet the home owners who don’t mind if their home falls in value Six parties bid on the Hoppers Crossing home, beginning at $770,000 and rising in $10,000 offers to $800,000. It then increased in $5000 and $1000 offers. An attempt to place a $100 bid was rejected. The new owners are moving from a three-bedroom to a five-bedroom house. “They like the location and want to stay in the same area,” Khan said.

Advertisement

The vendors are moving to be closer to their children’s schools. Khan said the market was all right in the $700,000-to-$750,000 range but slower above. Sellers have the most success with buyers “if a property is priced well and they can see the value, especially with the land”, he said. LJ Hooker head of research Mathew Tiller said Melbourne’s auction clearance rate showed the market was “a little bit soft at the moment”. “But the 55 per cent result demonstrates that there still are sales occurring and people turning up to auctions,” he said. “It is not a dire result but a little bit soft.” Tiller said the number of properties coming onto the market was slowing down as owners hesitated amid the economic uncertainty.

title: Fresh spike in bird flu cases in one state
text:
Bird flu cases have spiked in South Australia with seven new cases now confirmed.

Federal Agricultural Minister Julie Collins said several terns had been sent to a CSIRO testing facility to understand how the deadly virus had been transmitted.

Seven new cases of bird flu have been reported in South Australia. Picture: NewsWire / Daniel Pockett

"We have overnight had seven further suspected cases from South Australia," Ms Collins said.

"These have now been raced off to the CSIRO laboratory in terms of determining whether or not … that means we have local transmission here in Australia or not."

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Ms Collins said detection had been identified along the South Australian coast and that the risk to human health remains low.

"I do want to reiterate that at this time there are no mass mortalities, there is no evidence of H5 bird flu in our poultry or agricultural systems and the risk to human health remains low," she said.

Of the seven cases recorded in South Australia, five came from the same site over a two-day period.

Ms Collins said the virus has been found in seabirds and migratory birds and she thanked the public for their help documenting the cases as they arose.

"We have always indicated that we couldn't stop it from arriving in Australia," she said.

Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said five of the new cases had come from the same site. Picture: NewsWire / Martin Ollman.

"This is something we have prepared for. We have been working with states and territories ... and the states and territories have been doing an enormous amount of triaging and testing right across the country."
